title: Kayd Coffman felt ‘calling’ to revive MSU football as young core steps up
summary: Freshman quarterback Kayd Coffman and a young core of Spartans, many from Michigan, look to build momentum in the season finale vs. Rutgers.
content: EAST LANSING — Kayd Coffman drove up to Michigan State’s campus and just looked around, unannounced. The towers of the T. B. Simon Power Plant peeked out over the tops of the buildings. The scoreboard of Spartan Stadium loomed over Shaw Lane. The MSU quarterback commit had long ago made up his mind: He was going to be a Spartan. This visit told him he needed to be. “It was just really calm,” Coffman recalled Tuesday, Nov. 24. “I truly felt that was the Holy Spirit calling me.” Coffman, speaking after Tuesday’s practice in an Athletes in Action ministries T-shirt, is a man of deep faith. And though nobody could have expected it back in August, he will make his third start of the season — barring significant injury updates — when Michigan State travels to Rutgers for a 4:15 p.m. on Saturday, Nov. 28. Michigan State (3-8, 1-7) will mark a fifth straight losing season under a third separate coach when the final whistle sounds in New Jersey. How much of that can be pinned on injury woes — 18 one-time starters missed at least one game this season — is impossible to determine. The silver lining of all those blows, though, is that some of the program’s younger contributors get to cut their teeth against Big Ten competition. More: Fitzgerald: Every Big Ten coach opposes current injury report rules For some players, reps have been there all season. Antonio Johnson has taken snaps as a sixth offensive lineman all season, while fellow Orchard Lake St. Mary’s product Jayden Savoury led the Big Ten in tight end receptions before an injury left his right foot braced on a scooter. Amid so many injuries, though, young guys have had to step up. Coffman (East Kentwood) at quarterback. Bryson Williams (Orchard Lake St. Mary’s) and Samson Gash (Detroit Catholic Central) at wide receiver. Derrick Simmons (Frankenmuth) at defensive tackle. That gives those players a look at what they’ll have to do to be difference makers, and MSU where exactly their talents stack up. “We weren’t all so perfect coming out of high school, so we had to get developed as well,” said Williams, who caught his second touchdown of the season Nov. 14 against Washington. “So that played a huge part of it. All of us, like, stayed the course and got developed, and with development and opportunity, we were able to make our plays.” The fruits of such workloads for young players can really be seen two, three, four years from now, which is an eternity in college football, much more so when the transfer portal gives no guarantees that any player will stay with a program the duration of his career. Coffman, at least, says he’s in it for the long haul. Last early signing day, days after Pat Fitzgerald replaced Jonathan Smith as head coach, he penned an open letter to fans in the Detroit Free Press committing himself to reviving “a program that has not been what it is supposed to be.” For various other reasons, a collection of in-state kids have banded together to form a young core for a Michigan State team that ranks fourth oldest among Power Four teams. At least 25 players will age out this offseason. That’s not counting any portal losses, which even Fitzgerald expects to see. But as he tries to build something in East Lansing, he is excited about younger players like Coffman and Williams. “It reminds me of my young experience as a player, when a lot of us played before we were ready,” said the former Northwestern linebacker. “And you know, you prefer to have those experiences in the winter and spring ball and training camp, but when it happens in the arena, you’re fired up, you’re excited, and then the reality sets in of how far you have to go to become the player you need to be, you’re capable of, for us to win at a high level.” The fact that many Michigan products are playing gives credence to his recruiting pitches to other in-state talents. Offensive linemen Grant Adloff (East Grand Rapids) and Jack Carlson (Brighton) are big additions in the class that will sign Wednesday, Dec. 2, and so is Detroit King safety Don Spillers. “We’re going to start our recruiting here in the state of Michigan, and I think we backed that up in our first class,” Fitzgerald said. “... The best players in the state, we’re gonna do everything we can to have them here at State, and that’s the bottom line.” Michigan State wants to harness in-state talent. It also wants to complement the roster with capable transfers, something that Fitzgerald hinted at earlier this season, and athletic director Dan Bartholomae all but promised to fund in a homecoming address to fans. Year-over-year retention, though, is needed for stability. More: AD Dan Bartholomae likes to work fast, but has big job at Michigan State Coffman is a big part of that. So is the growth his coaches saw between his first two starts, and where it might continue Saturday in New Jersey. “That’s what you’re always hoping for as a coach is that those in-game reps and experiences, that they can learn from them,” offensive coordinator Nick Sheridan said. “You know, the game can often reveal where you’re at in your journey.” Through a couple of intimidating starts at UCLA in the Rose Bowl — “my family was able to fly out, so that was a really fun experience,” Coffman said — and last week against Oregon , the freshman quarterback took his lumps. He threw four completions and a touchdown to start his career, then threw 10 straight incompletions across appearances in three games. He has two picks on the season, one trying to throw into the field instead of working the boundary, and one on an ill-advised throw last week. Rutgers will be a tamer threat, even on the road. With no shot at a bowl for either team hanging in the balance, there’s still pride on the line, whatever is left this late in a dead season. “Our focus right now is on finishing the right way,” Fitzgerald said. Because even if this is only a sneak peek at the future, it’s one Michigan State needs to see. Michigan State at Rutgers ▶ Kick: 4:15 p.m., Saturday, Nov. 28, SHI Stadium, Piscataway, N.J. ▶ TV/radio: Big Ten Network/760-AM ▶ Records: Michigan State 3-8, 1-7 Big Ten; Rutgers 3-8, 2-6 ▶ Line: Michigan State by 3½. ▶ Series: MSU leads, 10-6. Last meeting: Rutgers won 41-14 at Spartan Stadium on Nov. 30, 2024 . cearegood@detroitnews.com @ConnorEaregood This article originally appeared on The Detroit News: Kayd Coffman felt ‘calling’ to revive MSU football as young core steps up

title: KJ Duff reflects on Rutgers football legacy as his NFL decision looms
summary: KJ Duff became one of the top receivers in Rutgers football history. What's next for the star wideout and NFL prospect? He reflects on that and more.
content: PISCATAWAY – All KJ Duff knew at the time was that he couldn’t finish the rest of the game. Rutgers football’s star wide receiver had reaggravated an injury during the Scarlet Knights ’ game against Michigan that he had suffered the week prior, but even as he walked off the SHI Stadium field the possibility he had played his last snap never crossed his mind. Then came the diagnosis of a high-ankle sprain, followed by surgery that would end his season four games too soon. “It definitely was frustrating,” Duff told USA TODAY-New Jersey this week. “All I really want to do is play football, and then that gets taken away.” Frustrating for Duff. Disappointing for the program. And perhaps more disappointing for a fanbase that, for three seasons, watched Duff develop into one of the best receivers in the program’s history, climbing lists in the record books, filling highlight reels with jaw-dropping catches and cementing a legacy that won’t soon be forgotten. Duff hasn’t officially announced his future – whether he’ll pursue the NFL or return to Rutgers for his final year of eligibility. But Duff is projected as a potential first-round draft pick. He’d become the first Rutgers player to hold that distinction since 2010. Coach Greg Schiano also said after a recent game that if Duff asked him, he’d advise him to pursue the NFL. If Duff makes that choice, Schiano made it clear he’ll miss having him in the program. The reasons why are clear. “I’ve told everybody that comes here, it was a lot of fun while it lasted because our hardest working player was our best player,” Schiano said. “That’s fun when you can point to him as an example. Especially in this era of so many newcomers, like, ‘Look what he’s doing, Try to do that.’” That work paid off. “It feels great to be recognized as that, but it's really about what you put into it,” Duff said. “I go with that mentality of, ‘I want to be great.’ I want to put myself in the best position to be successful.” Duff said his focus now is on getting healthy, which was off to a good start just more than two weeks after surgery. Duff said he was already doing some jogging and his doctors said he’s ahead of schedule in his recovery after initially saying he’d be able to resume football activities in January. “I don't want to rush anything and put myself in a bad position,” Duff said. KJ Duff stayed loyal to Rutgers football and developed into a star receiver Duff, who joined the program as the top overall recruit in New York for the 2024 recruiting class out of St. Anthony's High School on Long Island, in three seasons at Rutgers had 132 catches for 2,283 yards with 17 touchdowns. In eight games this season before getting hurt, Duff had 774 receiving yards on 45 catches with a season-high nine touchdowns. He had at least 100 receiving yards in four of those games. He ranks seventh in program history in career yards and is tied for fifth in touchdowns and 10 th in receptions. Duff established his legacy – doing that only at Rutgers was important to him. “The people, as in the coaches, the players, everybody here, (the program) really does mean a lot, and that's ultimately why I chose to come back this year,” Duff said. “Because in life you need to have substance. You can't just chase everything around. This is what made me happy and what I ultimately wanted to do.” So while programs around the country would've loved to land Duff as a transfer, he ultimately chose to stick with the only program he's known. “You can go be a one-year rental, essentially, somewhere else,” Duff said. “New place, leave all your legacy behind and just play that one season there maybe for a new uniform or a bigger stadium perhaps. But, like I said, in life, you need substance. Stuff that is actually important to you, and you’ve got to value that. And ultimately that’s the coaches here who I was getting coached by, my teammates who I was going to be able to play with.” Schiano played a pivotal role in Duff remaining at Rutgers. “Coach Schiano, I can't even put it in words,” Duff said. “That's the type of leader he is. How much he truly cares about the players. I always admired him for that. And just the way the program is, the blue collar, hardworking (culture), I really appreciate that. Because that's real hard work. That goes to chop and everything he preaches, the hard-nosed mentality. That really prepares you for life.” Where KJ Duff improved the most at Rutgers Duff joined Rutgers as a high-level recruit and played well as a true freshman – but he only improved since and became one of the top receivers in the country. Wide receivers coach Dave Brock oversaw that development and helped turn Duff into a potential first-round draft pick. “He's coached some of the best around, so he knows what it knows what it takes, knows what it should look like, knows what it should sound like,” Duff said. “Sound, it's a big thing, because when you're playing and you want to make a cut, you should be able to close your eyes and just hear how powerful your feet are in the ground. That’s a big thing that he talks about. If you're just tiptoeing around, you have no power in the ground.” That’s why Brock told Duff after his freshman season he had to get stronger in his lower half. Duff attacked that in the offseason. The work turned Duff into a more explosive, powerful receiver. “If you look at me releasing at the line of scrimmage from my freshman year to now, I think it's a huge difference,” Duff said. Along the way Duff made things easier for his quarterback, and delighted the Rutgers fanbase with catches that will be shown on the videoboard for years to come. At a time when players bounce from program to program, Duff never did. He stayed loyal, stayed with the program and the coaches that recruited him and developed him. At some point in the future – very possibly the near future – Rutgers fans will be watching him on Sundays while remembering the consistency he delivered for a program that went through its share of ups and downs during his three seasons. Duff wanted to leave a legacy. He did exactly that. “I think that's everything,” Duff said. “That's truly like why I wanted to stay. I go back to substance. That's what I wanted for myself. That's how I wanted to be remembered. The fact that I was able to do that in, it feels great. That's truly what my goal was.” This article originally appeared on Asbury Park Press: KJ Duff reflects on Rutgers football legacy as his NFL decision looms

title: Louisville flips 4-star DL Jamar Thompson from Georgia Tech after official visit
summary: Louisville's persistence paid off. Four-star defensive lineman Jamar Thompson has flipped his commitment from Georgia Tech to the Cardinals following an official visit. Mark Ivey played a key role in the recruiting victory, and Thompson's high school coach explains what makes the Florida standout special and why he could thrive.
content: Louisville turned up the heat on Jamar Thompson this fall, and Jeff Brohm and his staff have landed another major recruiting victory. The four-star defensive lineman out of Boca Raton (Fla.) West Boca Raton has flipped his commitment from Georgia Tech to Louisville following an official visit earlier this week. Thompson committed to the Yellow Jackets over the summer. He had strong relationships with Brent Key and his staff, then Georgia Tech struggled this season and Thompson kept his ear open. Louisville defensive line coach Mark Ivey increased his communication with the Florida standout. The relationship grew, the Cardinals gained momentum and Thompson agreed to take an official visit. After playing Saturday, Thompson traveled to Louisville for a Sunday-Monday visit. The experience sealed the deal. Thompson loved the visit, connected with the people inside the program and left excited about what Brohm is building at Louisville. With signing day approaching, the Cardinals have added another premier defensive lineman to their 2027 recruiting class. High school coach sees immediate impact potential West Boca Raton head coach Dylan Potts has watched Thompson develop into one of Florida’s premier defensive linemen. His physical tools stand out, but Potts believes Thompson’s approach to the game separates him from other talented prospects. “Jamar is a great kid, a very hard worker and has earned everything he’s got,” Potts told Rivals. “He’s one of the most physically talented defensive tackles in the country with his size and speed. “Matching that with his work ethic and ambition to continue getting better every year and not get complacent ever is what makes him special.” Thompson brings an intriguing combination of size, athleticism and explosiveness to Louisville’s defensive front. Potts believes his impact could come sooner rather than later. “Jamar has the ability to make an impact on the college scene right away next year,” Potts said. The opportunity to develop under Ivey and compete alongside other talented defensive linemen appeals to Thompson. Louisville’s coaching staff has earned the confidence of his high school coach, too. “Louisville has a great staff, and I know Coach Brohm and his staff are going to get the best out of Jamar,” Potts said. Louisville adds another West Boca Raton standout Thompson will have a familiar face waiting for him when he arrives at Louisville. Former West Boca Raton teammate and four-star cornerback Jaydin Broadnax is already with the Cardinals. That connection gave Thompson another level of familiarity with the program throughout the recruiting process. “Our four-star cornerback Jaydin Broadnax is up at Louisville from last year, so it is great to have another West Boca player up there with him,” Potts said. Now that reunion will happen. Louisville has established a connection with one of Florida’s top high school programs, and Thompson gives the Cardinals another talented piece on defense.

title: Luke Moga Prepares for Second Start as Lobos Eye Mountain West Championship Hosting Rights
summary: ALBUQUERQUE, N.M. (KRQE) –The stakes are high for the University of New Mexico football team heading into Friday’s matchup against Air Force, and quarterback Luke Moga will be back under center for his second collegiate start. The Mountain West-leading Lobos can secure the right to host the Mountain West Championship Game with a victory over […]
content: ALBUQUERQUE, N.M. (KRQE) –The stakes are high for the University of New Mexico football team heading into Friday's matchup against Air Force, and quarterback Luke Moga will be back under center for his second collegiate start. The Mountain West-leading Lobos can secure the right to host the Mountain West Championship Game with a victory over the Falcons at University Stadium. Moga made the most of his first collegiate start, leading New Mexico to a road win over then-first-place Wyoming. He threw for 234 yards and a touchdown while adding another score on the ground. Despite the strong debut, Moga isn't satisfied with his performance. He's focused on improving his timing with receivers and making the most of every opportunity. "Yeah, I think just some timing things with guys, with receivers, and some things that I can do better," Moga said. "We can push depth on routes, so them expecting the ball and me putting it on them. There are some scramble opportunities. So every completion matters in this game." Moga also said he feels good about the team's progress heading into Friday's matchup, noting that the Lobos are getting players back healthier. Air Force will present another major challenge for New Mexico. The Falcons bring one of the Mountain West's top defenses to Albuquerque, allowing just 18.1 points and 273 yards per game. Air Force ranks among the nation's top five teams in passing defense and sits second in the Mountain West in that category. The Lobos will look to take advantage of home-field support while continuing their push toward a conference championship. Kickoff is scheduled for 2:30 p.m. Friday at University Stadium. title: Offensive Players to Watch as Tulane Gears Up for South Florida Contest
summary: The Green Wave will look to end the regular season with a strong conference win.
content: The Tulane Green Wave will look to end the regular season on a high note as it takes on the South Florida Bulls on Saturday. The Green Wave hasn't had the season it wanted, but younger talent has shown that there can still be a bright future for the program. The team is coming off a 28-24 win over the North Texas Mean Green; though that victory came against a significantly hindered UNT team, Tulane still had to find a way to dig deep and battle from behind. The Wave now turns its attention to one final regular season test ahead of a potential bowl appearance. Here's a look at which offensive players could make the biggest difference for Tulane on Saturday. QB Trace Johnson As expected, Johnson has had some growing pains, but he had his best outing of the season last weekend against the Mean Green. The true freshman signal-caller completed 17 of his 21 pass attempts for 283 yards and four touchdowns, demonstrating poise and confidence as he led his team on a game-winning drive with just over two minutes remaining in the game. Johnson was named to the American Conference Weekly Honor Roll in recognition of his strong performance. There's no doubt that this kid has talent and can be the future of the program -- imagine just how much he can grow this offseason. For now, he's focused on capping off a freshman season that he'll never forget. RB Jaylin Lucas Lucas has been quiet since his hot start to the season, but he contributed in more ways than one against North Texas. The running back led all players with 46 rushing yards on five carries, but he also caught three passes for 79 yards and a touchdown. Lucas showed his versatility in a big way and continually put his team in position to succeed. What more could you ask for from a veteran player? It's vital that Lucas continues this momentum as he returns to the Sunshine State. Expect him to give it his all this weekend. TE Cameron Roberts Roberts came out of nowhere last weekend. The tight end has been quiet all season, but he put together an outstanding game with a team-high 81 yards and two touchdowns on four receptions. It was his best showing of the year by a long shot, and it couldn't have come at a better time. On top of this, Roberts is just a freshman -- he's got plenty of years of college football ahead of him. If last weekend was any indication of what Greenies can expect from him moving forward, well, then he has the chance to be a pivotal part of the offense for years to come.

title: Ohio State’s entire football program needs a reset, and it needs to start on Sunday
summary: Ohio State cannot simply rely on what made it successful in a bygone era. It needs to change how it operates if it wants to remain amongst college football’s elite. Beat TTUN on Saturday. Reset the program on Sunday.
content: LOS ANGELES, CALIFORNIA - OCTOBER 31: Ryan Day of the Ohio State Buckeyes reacts to a call during the game against the USC Trojans at Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum on October 31, 2026 in Los Angeles, California. (Photo by Ben Liebenberg/Getty Images) | Getty Images I love Ohio State football, I love Ohio State basketball, I love Buckeye Donuts, I love Mirror Lake, I love Orton Hall, I love “Carmen Ohio,” I love the Skull Session, I love TBDBITL, I love The Ohio State University. Being a Buckeye is not something I chose; it is who I am. My parents met as students at Ohio State, I grew up in Central Ohio, and I am a damn proud Ohio State alum. Even though I have now lived outside of Ohio for more of my life than I have inside the Buckeye State, I still bleed scarlet and gray with every bit of the passion that I did as a freshman looking out my dorm room window on the 21st floor of Lincoln Tower as The Best Damn Band in the Land practiced in the field below. So, I take absolutely no joy in writing about the decline of Ohio State’s football program or the years of squandered opportunities that preceded it. But, just as you would with someone you love, I feel compelled to offer the tough love that, at least from where I sit, Ryan Day, Ross Bjork, and everyone else in positions of power at the Woody Hayes Athletic Center desperately need to hear. The entire Ohio State football program needs a reset, and regardless of what happens against That Team Up North tomorrow, that process needs to begin on Sunday morning, if not Saturday night. I have no idea who will be Ohio State’s head football coach in 2027. I suppose that since I don’t foresee a scenario in which Bjork fires Day, the only way that someone new is leading the program next season is if Day decides to leave of his own volition. Given the immense pressures and personal strains that come with coaching at Ohio State, that wouldn’t completely shock me, but I am operating under the assumption that both Day and Bjork will be back next year. Unfortunately, I have increasingly little faith in either man’s ability to recognize the magnitude of the changes that need to be made. Both seem to be operating under the assumption that the principles and practices that got Ohio State to the mountaintop in a previous era of college football will keep them there in today’s wildly different one. They simply will not. Day has accomplished things at Ohio State that the overwhelming majority of college football coaches will never come close to achieving. He has won a national championship, competed for another, recruited and developed exceptional talent, and overseen some of the most explosive offenses in program history. Those accomplishments deserve both recognition and appreciation, but they do not invalidate the markedly diminishing returns that we have seen throughout his tenure. Certainly, not everything that has gone wrong this season can be blamed on coaching, and I am sympathetic to the challenges presented by talent lost to the NFL and injuries at the most important positions on the field. But this season did not create my concerns about the direction of the program out of whole cloth; it crystallized them. College football has undergone a fundamental transformation over the past five years, and the advantages that once virtually guaranteed Ohio State a place amongst the sport’s elite no longer do. The transfer portal has changed how rosters are constructed, NIL and revenue sharing have changed how players are acquired and retained, and the expanded playoff has changed how championship contenders need to manage an entire season. Ohio State has certainly participated in — and even benefited from — those changes, but participating in them and adapting to them are two very different things. The first order of business this offseason needs to be establishing a coherent football identity, because for years, the way that Day has constructed his roster has seemed to be at odds with how he has coached it. Ever since then-TTUN offensive coordinator Josh Gattis dismissed Ohio State as a finesse team that lacked toughness following the 2021 edition of The Game, it feels as though Day has been preoccupied with proving otherwise , often at the expense of the very things that made his teams so successful early in his tenure. What the hell is wrong with being a finesse football team when you are exceptionally good at it? Speed, precision, creativity, and athleticism are not liabilities, and none of them is incompatible with physical toughness. There is nothing inherently tough about repeatedly running the ball into the strength of an opponent’s defense, just as there is nothing inherently soft about getting the ball to a wide receiver whom nobody in the country can cover. Rather than maximizing the advantages afforded to him by Ohio State’s recruiting prowess, Day has too often asked his players to conform to an offensive philosophy that minimizes them. If you are going to devote considerable resources to assembling one of the most talented wide receiver rooms in the country, why are you so determined to run as few offensive plays as possible and to pull your best players off the field in favor of tight ends who seem incapable of blocking or catching? The same disconnect has become increasingly apparent on defense. Matt Patricia did a tremendous job with last year’s unit, but without that extraordinary collection of NFL-ready talent at his disposal, he has increasingly defaulted to passivity. I understand the schematic value of rushing three, disguising coverages, and limiting explosive plays, but when your defense cannot consistently generate pressure, there is nothing particularly safe about giving opposing quarterbacks all day to throw. No matter how good your secondary is — and I do think it is one of the strengths of OSU’s team — you cannot consistently expect defensive backs to maintain coverage when opposing quarterbacks have that much time to throw. Ohio State has surrendered at least 30 points in three of its last four games. At some point, the potential consequences of being more aggressive should become less concerning than the actual consequences of being conservative. If Ohio State wants to play a more methodical, possession-oriented brand of football, then take a page out of Kirk Ferentz’s book at Iowa and build a roster specifically designed to excel at it. Personally, I would much rather see the Buckeyes embrace the exceptional athletic talent that they are uniquely positioned to attract and force opposing coaches to spend their weeks figuring out how to account for Ohio State’s strengths, rather than the other way around. Establishing that identity will require a substantial overhaul of the coaching staff. As Day nears the end of his eighth full season as Ohio State’s head coach, it increasingly feels as though complacency and stubbornness have replaced the creativity and tenacity that marked the early years of his tenure. If he returns, retain the three or four position coaches who have consistently demonstrated an ability to develop talent and get the most out of their players, and replace the rest. But more important than simply bringing in new coaches is bringing in coaches with new ideas, people who will challenge Day’s thinking rather than kowtow to it. Hiring someone because he fits comfortably into an operation that is no longer producing acceptable results seems entirely counterproductive. This staff desperately needs a squeaky wheel, someone who will push back on the standard operating procedure that has led to a team seemingly in freefall. I generally don’t believe in judging a coordinator on a single season, especially when he had little involvement in constructing the roster that he inherited. So, if I had to retain one of Ohio State’s coordinators, I would probably give Arthur Smith another opportunity, although I am hardly passionate about that proposition. Despite the offense’s shortcomings and the difficult circumstances at quarterback, I at least saw efforts to adapt throughout the season. Conversely, over the past month, Patricia has continued to do the same things over and over again with increasingly frustrating results. There also needs to be a fundamental reassessment of how Ohio State evaluates, acquires, develops, and retains talent. On Thanksgiving, five-star defensive end DJ Jacobs, the No. 1 player in the 2027 recruiting class according to Rivals, flipped his commitment from Ohio State to Miami, joining Mark Fletcher Jr., Justin Scott, and Jordan Lyle as prominent prospects to have decommitted from the Buckeyes in favor of the Hurricanes in the past five recruiting cycles alone. Fletcher, of course, went on to be named the offensive MVP of the Cotton Bowl last season, in which Miami ended Ohio State’s national title defense. And those are just the guys that OSU has lost to the Canes, to say nothing of Oregon’s Na’eem Offord and Jeremiah McClellan, USC’s Kayden Dixon-Wyatt, Maryland’s Zahir Mathis, Auburn’s Blake Woodby, and Georgia’s Jontae Gilbert. Recruiting losses are inevitable, especially in this era of college football, but when you continue to lose top players in the same fashion, at what point do you determine that there is something deficient in your process? Day, Mark Pantoni, and the entire personnel operation need to figure out why they are struggling to close on some of their most coveted prospects and, perhaps more concerningly, why they are struggling to hold onto some of the ones they already landed. As is true with all things in college football these days, money undoubtedly plays a role. But it cannot simply be hand-waved away as “Miami offered more money.” This is Ohio State we’re talking about, an athletic department that generated a record $336.1 million in revenue fiscal year 2025, including more than $68 million in donor-funded contributions. If Ohio State cannot consistently translate its considerable financial advantages into recruiting success, that itself warrants a reassessment of how the program operates. However, Day has made retaining established talent a priority, and philosophically, I don’t disagree with him. I would much rather root for a team built primarily around players who have spent several years in Columbus than one that is reconstructed through the transfer portal every January. There is considerably less financial risk in investing in a proven college football player than there is in investing in a high school prospect. But when you miss on players like David Gabriel Georges and lose commitments from players like Jacobs, who exactly are you setting aside all of that money to retain? This isn’t necessarily about how much Ohio State is spending, but how effectively it is allocating its resources. You cannot sustain a roster retention strategy without continuing to acquire and develop players worth retaining, and every recruiting shortcoming potentially becomes a more expensive problem to solve in the transfer portal. Beyond the personnel decisions, I want an exhaustive examination of how this program prepares to play football games. How are practices structured? How are game plans developed? How are backups prepared to contribute? Who is responsible for identifying schematic problems during games, and who has the authority to correct them? How does the program evaluate whether a player’s lack of development is a failure of recruiting, coaching, or effort? The fact that we have been having many of the same conversations about Ohio State football for the better part of five years suggests that the program’s greatest deficiency might be its inability to diagnose and correct its own deficiencies. That is where Bjork needs to assert himself as the athletic director. If he believes that Day is the right person to lead Ohio State football into its next era, then it is incumbent upon him to establish the expectations, demand the organizational changes, and enforce the accountability necessary to ensure that Day actually does so. Unfortunately, nothing in this man’s résumé gives me any confidence that putting him in charge of a football program will lead to anything good. After all, he helped orchestrate the contract extension that ultimately saddled Texas A&M with Jimbo Fisher’s $77 million buyout, and he oversaw Ole Miss during the Hugh Freeze recruiting scandal and the subsequent legal battle that ended with the university having to formally apologize to Houston Nutt. The irony, of course, is that we have already seen what Day’s program is capable of when it is willing to challenge its own assumptions. Following the disastrous loss to Michigan in 2024, the Buckeyes had some difficult, emotionally charged conversations that preceded one of the most spectacular stretches of football that any of us have ever had the privilege of watching. That national championship run should have provided the roadmap for how Ohio State could become the preeminent program in college football for the next decade. Instead, we are less than two years removed from the title, and the Buckeyes are 5-6 against their last 11 Power Four opponents. Somehow, the lessons that Ohio State learned during the most successful month of Day’s coaching career have failed to become part of how he handles his business on a daily basis. The championship run should have been a reminder that creativity, aggression, and tenacity are how you make the most of an uber-talented team. Instead, he has reverted to the frustratingly conservative practices that made a near-mutiny necessary in the first place. Moreover, Ohio State cannot continue to require a crisis in order to summon the best version of itself. The willingness to challenge established practices, confront uncomfortable truths, and change course when necessary needs to be a foundational component of the program’s culture, not a last-ditch emergency measure. I fully recognize that we live a charmed existence as Ohio State football fans, and I understand how obnoxious it must sound to fans of practically any other program to hear us complain less than two years removed from winning a national championship. But there is a difference between expecting Ohio State to win every game and expecting Ohio State to consistently give itself the best possible opportunity to win every game. It is the latter expectation that I believe this program has failed to meet far too often under Day. And despite my waning confidence in Day and Bjork, I am willing to grant them both the time and the grace necessary to get this thing right. I would willingly endure a rebuilding season in 2027 if it meant that Ohio State was purging the program of its outdated habits and philosophies, empowering new people with new ideas, and establishing a culture built around a fresh vision for how to win championships in modern college football. I would be far more encouraged by a young, imperfect team that improves throughout the season, establishes a clear identity, and demonstrates a discernible upward trajectory than I would be by a more experienced team that wins 10 games in spite of the same coaching and organizational issues that have torpedoed the last two seasons. I can stomach losing games as part of a deliberate effort to build something better; what I cannot stomach is continuing to lose games because the people in charge are unwilling or unable to recognize that something needs to change. There is no shame in acknowledging that approaches that once made you successful are no longer doing so, but there is considerable shame in clinging to remnants of bygone eras as the program deteriorates around you. Tomorrow, I want nothing more than to watch the Buckeyes beat the hell out of the Corn and Blue. I want the players to experience the joy of winning The Game at home , and I want every scarlet and gray-clad person in Ohio Stadium to celebrate a victory that is woefully overdue. But a win cannot be allowed to absolve the program of its shortcomings, just as another loss should not be necessary to convince its leadership that substantive changes are required. Get new ideas and new people into the Woody. Establish new processes for recruiting, development, preparation, and evaluation. Build a new identity that capitalizes on Ohio State’s extraordinary advantages rather than one that assumes those advantages will perpetually insulate the program from the consequences of its own mistakes. Ohio State does not need to lower its expectations to accommodate the changing realities of college football; it needs to change the way that it operates in order to continue meeting — and, Woody forbid, exceeding — those expectations. Go beat your rival on Saturday afternoon, celebrate the hell out of it on Saturday night, and get to work building the next era of Ohio State football dominance on Sunday morning. Go Bucks. Beat Michigan.

title: How can Ohio State football beat Michigan? 3 keys for annual rivalry game
summary: Ohio State ends the regular season against archrival Michigan. Here are the keys to a second straight win in The Game.
content: Here are three keys for No. 21 Ohio State against Michigan on Nov. 28: Salvage pride This is the first time in the Ryan Day era that the Buckeyes face their archrivals without meaningful postseason implications. There is no real path for the Buckeyes to make the College Football Playoff or reach the Big Ten championship game, barring an extreme set of circumstances. All that’s at stake this weekend is potential bragging rights. Is that enough? The Buckeyes could save face in a lost season by defeating Michigan in consecutive years for the first time since their eight-game winning streak during the 2010s. But they’ll need to dig deep and channel their disappointment toward beating the team that matters the most on their schedule. Stop the run Michigan’s offense has run through freshman running back Savion Hiter in recent weeks. He was instrumental in last week’s upset of UCLA, rushing for 104 yards on 26 carries. It was his second straight 100-yard game. Hiter is a bruising runner who has picked up 194 of his 212 rushing yards after contact over the last two games, according to Pro Football Focus. The Buckeyes will need to find ways to bring him to the ground after they struggled to tackle Nebraska’s Jamal Rule in their previous loss. If they hold up in the trenches, it’ll put pressure on Michigan’s passing game, which averages the fewest yards per game among Power 4 teams. Win the turnover battle Sloppiness might be inevitable in a matchup of teams with the worst turnover margins in the Big Ten since the start of conference play. Ohio State isn’t as mistake prone as Michigan, but its defense rarely generates takeaways. While the Buckeyes have created only four turnovers in their last six games, the Wolverines forced a season-high three against UCLA, including a recovered fumble by quarterback Ty Dieffenbach that positioned them for their lone touchdown. Short fields are boon for any offense, but they would especially benefit Michigan, which has had trouble sustaining drives. The Buckeyes can ill afford to set up the Wolverines in plus territory and gift possessions. Key matchup Ohio State offensive line vs. Michigan defensive line When the Buckeyes snapped their four-game losing streak in The Game last November, the offensive line played a significant role. It provided quarterback Julian Sayin with a clean pocket and controlled the line of scrimmage for the running game to put the game away in the second half. The position group has taken a step back this year despite personnel continuity, but it will need to respond to the challenge against one of the best defensive fronts in the country. Michigan entered the last weekend of the regular season as one of only 11 FBS teams to allow less than 3 yards per carry. Utah transfer defensive end John Henry Daley has also anchored the pass rush. It’s paramount that the Buckeyes hold up in the trenches in order stay on schedule and protect freshman quarterback Luke Fahey. Key stat 9: Combined losses between Ohio State and Michigan, the most entering The Game since 2008. Joey Kaufman covers Ohio State football for The Columbus Dispatch. Email him at jkaufman@dispatch.com and follow him on @joeyrkaufman on X. title: Ohio State football Michigan hype video: 'FIGHT LIKE HELL'
summary: Ohio State dropped its Michigan-week trailer Thursday. Fire, legends, and one message: FIGHT LIKE HELL. The Game kicks off Saturday at noon on FOX.
content: It's here. The Ohio State vs. Michigan trailer dropped Thursday, right on schedule for game week, and it does exactly what a Michigan-week trailer is supposed to do. It reminds you what this game is. And it doesn't ask politely. Ohio State vs. Michigan trailer opens with fire and Buckeye legends The video opens with fire and sparks over helmets. Then the names start flashing across the screen. CJ Barnett. Nolan Baudo. Maurice Clarett. Ryan Day. Archie Griffin. Woody Hayes. James Laurinaitis. Mickey Marotti. Urban Meyer. Jim Tressel. That's the point, and the trailer doesn't hide it. This game belongs to the people who built it. From there it moves fast. Archival footage and recent highlights cut together -- hard hits, touchdowns, celebrations, crowd shots from both sides. The marching band. The Block O. Player close-ups. Campus landmarks. Historical photos. The whole thing is stitched together with voiceover that frames The Game as something bigger than a football game. "The greatest robbery in all of sport." "A vendetta of hatred." "Our culture versus their culture." "For the brotherhood." One line lands harder than the rest. The preparation lasts 364 days. The game lasts 60 minutes. The stadiums, the narration says, are cathedrals built with "blood, sweat, sacrifice." A countdown clock reads "THE GREATEST RIVALRY SINCE OCTOBER 16, 1897." Brick walkways are marked "HATE." And it all ends where it has to end, with three words on the screen and the Block O behind them. FIGHT LIKE HELL. Ohio State vs. Michigan: what the trailer means for Saturday Now, look. A hype video doesn't block anybody. It doesn't cover Jeremiah Smith . It doesn't fix a defense that gave up 31 points at Nebraska . But this one is honest about what Saturday actually is. Ohio State is 7-4. Michigan is 6-5. There is no Big Ten title on the line. There is no College Football Playoff berth on the line. There is only the rivalry, and in this rivalry, that has always been enough. Embedded content: https://buckeyeswire.usatoday.com/story/sports/college/buckeyes/football/2025/11/29/ohio-state-michigan-reaction-5-takeaways-buckeyes-2025/87528657007/ Ryan Day is 2-4 against Michigan. The Buckeyes won in Ann Arbor last year, 27-9, snapping a four-game losing streak in the series. A win Saturday would give Ohio State back-to-back wins over the Wolverines for the first time since 2018-19, and it would do it at home, at noon, in front of a Horseshoe that has been waiting all year for this one. That's what the trailer is selling. Not a playoff run. Not a trophy. Just the game itself, and the 364 days that go into 60 minutes of it. Watch the trailer, then get ready. Saturday can't get here fast enough. Score Prediction: Ohio State 20, Michigan 17 Contact/Follow us @BuckeyesWire on X (formerly Twitter) and like our page on Facebook to follow ongoing coverage of Ohio State news, notes and opinion. Follow Phil Harrison on X: @PhilHarrisonBW . This article originally appeared on Buckeyes Wire: Ohio State football Michigan hype video: 'FIGHT LIKE HELL'

title: Ohio State vs. Michigan: 2026 game preview and prediction
summary: Ohio State close out their 2026 regular season campaign with their annual clash against Michigan. The Buckeyes hope to out last week’s loss behind them and make it two straight over the Wolverines
content: EUGENE, OR - NOVEMBER 14: Michigan Wolverines quarterback Bryce Underwood (19) rolls out to pass against Oregon Ducks defensive lineman D'Antre Robinson (0) during a college football game between the Oregon Ducks and Michigan Wolverines on November 14, 2026 at Autzen Stadium in Eugene, Oregon. (Photo by Brian Murphy/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Ohio State and Michigan will meet on the gridiron on Saturday for the 122nd time in the storied rivalry. This year doesn’t have quite as much juice as in years past, since both teams enter The Game with at least four losses. With the Buckeyes and Wolverines both out of the Big Ten title and College Football Playoff race, the two squads will only have pride to play for on Saturday afternoon in Columbus. A disappointing season in Columbus The Buckeyes limp into their final game of the regular season having lost three of their last four games. The latest of those losses came last week when they fell 31-28 at Nebraska. Had Ohio State beaten the Cornhuskers, then the Buckeyes would likely not only have been ranked in the top-12 of the College Football Playoff rankings, but they would have also moved closer to making their second consecutive Big Ten Championship Game after both Indiana and UCLA lost last week. This marks the first season Ohio State has had at least four losses in a season since 2011, when the Buckeyes finished 6-7 with Luke Fickell as interim head coach. Following the loss to the Wolverines in 2011, Ohio State announced the hiring of Urban Meyer just a few days later. This year, Buckeye Nation is wondering what the future holds for Ryan Day and his coaching staff following The Game. Ohio State will be looking to edge closer to evening up the series with Michigan. Currently, the Buckeyes trail the Wolverines 53-62-6 after last year’s 27-9 win in Ann Arbor. The victory snapped Michigan’s four-game winning streak in the series. Since 2000, the Buckeyes have had the advantage in the series, winning 18 of the 25 meetings with the Wolverines. Jeremiah or bust on offense The best player on the field on Saturday will undoubtedly be Ohio State wide receiver Jeremiah Smith. The junior was named a finalist for both the Maxwell and Biletnikoff awards earlier this week and is currently the favorite to win the Heisman Trophy. After hauling in five passes for 165 yards and two touchdowns last week, Smith enters this game leading the country with 1,482 yards receiving and 17 touchdowns. The future NFL first-round pick’s 86 receptions this year are just four behind FAU’s Easton Messer for most in 2026 by an FBS receiver. Since arriving at Ohio State in 2024, Smith has hauled in 249 passes for 4,040 yards and 44 scores. Along with already setting Ohio State’s career receiving records for catches, yards, and touchdown receptions, Smith is just nine catches, 125 yards, and one touchdown catch shy of reaching the school’s single-season marks. Smith will need to get those numbers on Saturday since it seems unlikely he would play in a bowl game this year with the Buckeyes not in the College Football Playoff. Even more incredible, given what Smith has done this year, is that opponents know he is getting the football and still can’t stop him. The Buckeyes haven’t been able to find a consistent second option behind the stud receiver. Devin McCuin is the only wide receiver with more than 11 catches this year. The UTSA transfer has caught 32 passes for 406 yards and three touchdowns. Chris Henry Jr. had some big plays early in the season but hasn’t lived up to the hype yet. Tight ends Nate Roberts and Mason Williams have combined to catch 29 passes and find the end zone four times. Throwing to Smith and company will be quarterback Luke Fahey, who will be making his fifth start of the season on Saturday. Fahey is coming off a performance against Nebraska where he threw for 259 yards, two scores, and a pick last week. Entering The Game, Fahey has 10 touchdowns and five interceptions in relief of Julian Sayin. For being put in a tough spot, having to start after Julian Sayin was injured late in the game against Indiana, Fahey hasn’t played bad in his freshman year. Fahey is just the fifth true freshman to start at quarterback for the Buckeyes. If Ohio State is going to win for the second straight season over Michigan, they’ll need another big effort from running back Bo Jackson. As a freshman, Jackson totaled over 150 yards in the 27-9 win over the Wolverines in Ann Arbor. The sophomore is within striking distance of his second straight 1,000-yard season in the ground, rolling up 851 yards rushing through the first 11 games of the season, finding the end zone nine times. Jackson has also become a safety valve for Fahey through the air, catching 15 passes in Fahey’s four starts. Unlike Jackson, who has been steady all season for Ohio State, Isaiah West has had a hard time gaining much traction in the backfield for the Buckeyes. West started the season as the third-string running back before the injury to Ja’Kobi Jackson. Over the last five games, West has had three games where he ran for at least 45 yards but also two where he has gone for 11 or less. Fumbles have been a recurring problem, as the sophomore from Philadelphia has lost three this season. Searching for answers on defense Receiving the bulk of the criticism for last week’s loss in Lincoln was the Buckeye defense, which failed to get off the field in critical spots. Because of their failures to get the football back in the hands of the offense, the Cornhuskers won the time of possession battle by more than 10 minutes. After getting after Northwestern’s quarterback two weeks ago, the Ohio State pass rush disappeared last week. The only sack of the game was registered by linebacker Riley Pettijohn, who now has three sacks this year, which is second on the team behind the five sacks Kenyatta Jackson Jr. has notched. One defensive lineman who had a good game last week was Jason Moore. The defensive tackle had seven tackles in the loss, giving him 29 stops on the season. When it comes to interior linemen, Eddrick Houston leads the team with 31 tackles. UCF transfer John Walker and Will Smith Jr. have also been solid at defensive tackle for the Buckeyes. A position that needs someone to step up on a more consistent basis is linebacker. Payton Pierce has 56 tackles, but it doesn’t feel like a lot of those are impact stops. Riley Pettijohn makes impact plays, but at times he disappears. Christian Alliegro has been one of the best transfers this year for Ohio State, which isn’t saying a whole lot. Unfortunately, Alliegro will miss Saturday’s game due to injury. TJ Alford has had moments but gets lost in the rotations at times. At least the secondary should be able to make some plays this week with Bryce Underwood quarterbacking the Wolverines. Safety Earl Little Jr. leads the team with 66 tackles, while fellow safety Jaylen McClain is the only Buckeye with multiple interceptions this year. When Jay Timmons is healthy, there’s no question he is the best player on the defense. Timmons has come up with plays in some of Ohio State’s biggest games when he is on the field, but he is also still just a freshman. Despite missing a few games, Timmons has broken up eight passes and forced two fumbles. Timmons carries a questionable injury tag into The Game. At cornerback, Jermaine Mathews Jr. and Devin Sanchez are hoping they can close out the regular season on a high note. Sanchez has been picked on at times this year and responded with six PBUs. Mathews has shown he can get into the backfield, registering 4.5 tackles for loss to go along with nine pass breakups. Michigan’s season so far Michigan enters The Game with a little bit of momentum after outlasting previously undefeated UCLA 18-16 in triple overtime last week in Ann Arbor. The Wolverines are now 6-5 in Kyle Whittingham’s first season at Michigan after coaching Utah for over 20 years. The win pushed Whittingham’s career coaching record to 183-93. The 2026 season has been an odd one for the Wolverines. It all started with a controversial win over Western Michigan, followed by a victory over Oklahoma at home. Michigan would go on to drop five of their next eight before the win over the Bruins. At least fans of the Wolverines got to storm the field after wins in their first and last home games of the season. Michigan is a tough watch on offense Offense has been the biggest issue for Michigan in 2026. Offensive coordinator Jason Beck was fired after the unit failed to meet expectations, leaving Jim Harding to take over as interim offensive coordinator. Michigan has scored at least 20 points in just three games this season. Bryce Underwood started the season at quarterback but hasn’t come anywhere close to meeting the massive amount of NIL money he was given. Underwood was so bad he was benched in favor of Tommy Carr, who started four games before Underwood returned as starter against UCLA. Against the Bruins, Underwood completed just 11 of his 24 pass attempts for 127 yards and a touchdown. The junior quarterback is completing just over 50 percent of his passes, tossing six touchdowns and six interceptions in 2026. Underwood will be looking to improve on last year’s performance in The Game, where he connected on just eight passes for 63 yards. Last week Underwood was without top receiver Andrew Marsh, who was serving a one-game suspension for an incident exposure charge from February. Marsh leads the Wolverines with 48 receptions this year. Also missing against the Bruins was JJ Buchanan. The wide receiver with 646 yards and five touchdowns on 40 catches is likely out for the rest of the season after suffering a shoulder injury. Buchanan caught the Hail Mary pass from Underwood at the end of the Western Michigan game. Marsh, Buchanan, Hogan Hansen, and running back Savion Hiter are the only Wolverines with at least 10 catches this year. Hansen is a tight end who has 13 catches for just 128 yards. In last week’s game against UCLA, fellow tight end Mason Bonner caught Michigan’s only touchdown of the game. Expect Savion Hiter to see the bulk of the carries on Saturday when Michigan runs the football. Hiter leads the team with 542 yards rushing across his freshman season. Last week Hiter finished with 104 yards on 26 carries, recording his second straight 100-yard rushing game. Jordan Marshall has five rushing touchdowns, but it is unclear if he will play this week after sitting out last week’s game. Bryson Kuzdzal has added 223 yards rushing this season. One reason Michigan has struggled on offense is because of an offensive line that has been dealing with injuries throughout the year. The constant has been center Jake Guarnera. Tackle Blake Frazier missed last week’s game, leading to Marky Walbridge stepping in opposite Evan Link at the other tackle spot. Manuel Beigel and Nathan Efobi started at the guard spots last week. Far from Tickle Bears on defense Had it not been for the Michigan defense, the Wolverines would be in big trouble this season. Defensive coordinator Jay Hill’s group has allowed more than 21 points in just one game this season. Last week Michigan forced three turnovers in the win over UCLA. The defensive line of the Wolverines is led by John Henry Daley, who followed Whittingham to Ann Arbor. After recording two sacks last week against UCLA, Daley now has eight sacks on the season to go along with two forced fumbles. On the other end of the defensive line for Michigan is Andrew Nichols, who has 6 tackles for loss and 3.5 sacks this year. Starting on the interior of the defensive line last week for the Wolverines were Enow Etta and Trey Pierce. Leading Michigan in tackles this year is linebacker Troy Bowles. After recording nine tackles last week against UCLA, Bowles now has 88 stops this year. Nathaniel Staehling has added 60 tackles and had a 79-yard interception return for a touchdown against Minnesota. Other linebackers who could see time on the field on Saturday are Chase Taylor and Aisha Moa. Taylor has 28 tackles and two sacks. Moa started his career at BYU before transferring to Michigan State last year and then crossing rivalry lines in the transfer portal following last season. Michigan’s most impactful defensive back is Chris Bracy. Following stops at UAB and Memphis, Bracy has 80 tackles, three sacks, two interceptions, and two forced fumbles in 2026. Rod Moore will start alongside Bracy at safety. Jyaire Hill will start at one of the cornerback spots. Hill has 48 tackles and five PBUs through 11 games. Zeke Berry will be the other starting cornerback. Like Hill, Berry has intercepted a pass this season. Prediction This year’s edition of The Game has a different feel to it since there aren’t any big stakes at risk besides bragging rights. This marks the first time since 2011 the Buckeyes have entered the matchup with Michigan with more than three losses. The quarterback matchup also leaves a lot to be desired. Luke Fahey is still finding his footing as a starter, and Bryce Underwood has been terrible throughout his two seasons at Michigan. The only saving grace in this game is Jeremiah Smith. This will likely be Smith’s last collegiate game. With a shot at winning this year’s Heisman Trophy, expect Smith to be targeted frequently throughout Saturday’s game. Michigan’s defense has the ability to make this a frustrating game for Buckeye Nation to endure. The best shot Ohio State will have to score is forcing Underwood into turnovers and giving the offense a short field. In the end, the Buckeyes have the edge because they will have a fire lit under them after a disappointing game last week. Ohio State closes out the regular season with a win at home before there are likely big changes announced in the coming weeks. LGHL score prediction: 28-13, Ohio State

title: Ole Miss Dominates to Capture Another Egg Bowl Victory
summary: Ole Miss delivered another memorable performance in the Egg Bowl, pulling away from Mississippi State in the second half to earn a convincing 41-17 victory Friday afternoon at Vaught-Hemingway Stadium. The Rebels entered the rivalry matchup looking to extend their winning streak against the Bulldogs, while Mississippi State hoped to finish its season with an upset and keep its bowl hopes alive. For much of…
content: Nov 21, 2026; Oxford, Mississippi, USA; Mississippi Rebels quarterback Trinidad Chambliss (6) passes the ball during the first quarter against the Wofford Terriers at Vaught-Hemingway Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Petre Thomas-Imagn Images Credit: IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect (Reuters) Ole Miss delivered another memorable performance in the Egg Bowl, pulling away from Mississippi State in the second half to earn a convincing 41-17 victory Friday afternoon at Vaught-Hemingway Stadium. The Rebels entered the rivalry matchup looking to extend their winning streak against the Bulldogs, while Mississippi State hoped to finish its season with an upset and keep its bowl hopes alive. For much of the first half, it looked like the Bulldogs might have a chance to accomplish that goal. However, Ole Miss found another gear after halftime and completely took control of the game. Mississippi State started quickly, taking a 7-3 lead in the second quarter after running back Fluff Bothwell broke free for a 16 yard touchdown. The Bulldogs added a field goal later in the quarter to extend their advantage to 10-6. Ole Miss struggled to turn its opportunities into touchdowns during the opening half. The Rebels managed two field goals from Lucas Carneiro but could not find the end zone before halftime. Mississippi State’s defense deserves credit for making life difficult for quarterback Trinidad Chambliss and keeping the Bulldogs in front. Ole Miss Takes Control After Halftime The second half was a completely different story. Chambliss helped Ole Miss take its first lead of the afternoon with a six yard touchdown pass to Horatio Fields early in the third quarter. The Rebels followed that score with another impressive drive, capped by a four-yard touchdown run from Joshua Dye to make it 20-10. Mississippi State refused to go away quietly. Quarterback Parker Puckett connected with Bothwell on a 12 yard touchdown pass early in the fourth quarter, cutting the deficit to just three points at 20-17. However, the Bulldogs’ comeback hopes quickly disappeared following one of the biggest plays of the afternoon. Blake Purchase Delivers the Game Changing Play With Mississippi State attempting to get the ball back and potentially take the lead, Puckett threw an interception to Ole Miss defensive lineman Blake Purchase. Purchase returned the interception 58 yards to the goal line, setting up Chambliss for a one-yard rushing touchdown on the following play. That score gave Ole Miss a 27-17 advantage with 10:30 remaining and completely shifted the momentum. The Rebels added two more touchdowns before the final whistle, including a 21 yard touchdown pass from Chambliss to Michael Smith and another short touchdown run by Dye. Chambliss and the Rebels Finish Strong Chambliss finished with 237 passing yards, two passing touchdowns and a rushing score. Dye contributed 91 rushing yards and two touchdowns, while Bothwell led Mississippi State with 129 rushing yards and two total touchdowns. The Ole Miss defense was equally impressive. The Rebels recorded seven sacks and 13 tackles for loss, consistently putting pressure on Puckett and making it difficult for Mississippi State to sustain drives. Ole Miss Claims Another Egg Bowl The victory improves Ole Miss to 8-4 overall and 5-4 in SEC play, while Mississippi State falls to 5-7 and finishes its season without bowl eligibility. More importantly, the Rebels have now won four consecutive Egg Bowls, continuing their recent dominance in one of college football’s fiercest rivalries. Mississippi State had its opportunities, but Ole Miss proved too much to handle when the game mattered most. content: MOBILE, Ala. (AP) — Keenan Phillips scored a 7-yard rushing touchdown with 1:46 left, Jayvon Henderson intercepted a pass in the end zone in the closing seconds and South Alabama beat Appalachian State 20-13 on Friday in the regular-season finale for both teams. South Alabama’s Cam Robinson picked off a pass in the end zone early in the fourth quarter and on App State’s next possession Jaquari Lewis was stopped for no gain on a fourth-and-inches run with 5:44 left to preserve a 13-all tie before Phillips capped an 11-play, 73-yard drive with the go-ahead touchdown. Bishop Davenport was 15-of-25 passing for 211 yards with a touchdown and an interception to go with 40 yards rushing on six carries for South Alabama (7-5, 5-3 Sun Belt Conference). James London, who kicked a 42-yard field goal in the second quarter, made a 29-yarder with about 6:49 remaining in the third that gave the Mountaineers a 13-10 lead. Lewis finished with 93 yards rushing and a TD on 23 carries for App State (7-5, 5-3). Malachi Singleton was 22-of-28 passing for 240 yards with two interceptions. Davenport threw a 6-yard touchdown pass to Everett Hunter that opened the scoring about 7 minutes into the game and Dylan Freebury kicked a 21-yard field goal with 2:46 left in the first quarter that gave the Jaguars a 10-0 lead. The Mountaineers fell to 5-1 when they rush for at least 100 yards and 6-2 in one-score games this season. Up next App State: Awaits a likely bowl bid. title: Tennessee rout win vs Vanderbilt football 60 years ago led to Vandy coach Jack Green's resignation
summary: Tennessee shut out Vanderbilt 28-0 in 1966 and Commodores' coach Jack Green resigned the following day.
content: The Vanderbilt vs. Tennessee football game in Nashville 60 years ago was the 60th game in the series and was lopsided, with the Vols firmly in control. Longtime Tennessean sports editor Raymond Johnson vividly described Tennessee’s dominance. He likened it to the Muhammad Ali (then Cassius Clay) vs. Cleveland Williams heavyweight title fight 10 days earlier. Ali debuted the Ali Shuffle in the bout, bloodied Williams' nose and knocked him to the canvas multiple times before a referee stopped the fight early in the third round. The Vols' 28-0 victory on Nov. 26, 1966 hardly captured just how thoroughly they controlled the game before 26,882 fans at Vanderbilt's Dudley Field. Tennessee, led by junior quarterback Dewey Warren, scored all of the Vols points by halftime, and coach Doug Dickey began substituting players in the second quarter. Warren ran for two first-quarter touchdowns. TENNESSEE-ALABAMA RIVALRY ORIGIN: How Tennessee football vs Alabama became a 'Third Saturday in October' tradition Dickey kept his backups on the field to start the second half, allowing Vanderbilt to take the first kickoff and drive to the Vols' 2-yard line. Tennessee's second unit defense stiffened there to preserve the shutout. The Vols improved to 7-3 and earned a berth in the Gator Bowl, where they played Syracuse. It was Vanderbilt's ninth straight loss after opening the season with a win over The Citadel. Vanderbilt coach Jack Green's final game was against Tennessee The Tennessean's John Bibb, who covered Vanderbilt at the time, reported three days before the game that Commodores coach Jack Green's resignation was imminent. The night after the Tennessee game, Green resigned after four seasons with a 7–29–4 record. In December, Arkansas assistant Johnny Majors interviewed for Vanderbilt's coaching vacancy but later withdrew from consideration. Fellow Arkansas assistant Bill Pace was subsequently hired to replace Green. Majors later returned to his alma mater, Tennessee, to become the Vols' coach. title: Tennessee's Arion Carter, DeSean Bishop remain questionable vs Vanderbilt
summary: Tennessee football running back DeSean Bishop and linebacker Arion Carter remain questionable against Vanderbilt.
content: Tennessee football running back DeSean Bishop and linebacker Arion Carter remain questionable against Vanderbilt. Bishop and Carter were listed again on the SEC student-athlete availability report on Nov. 26. It will be updated daily and finalized 90 minutes before the game. No. 7 Tennessee (9-2, 6-2 SEC) must beat Vanderbilt (4-7, 1-7) in the regular-season finale on Nov. 28 (7 p.m. ET, ESPN) to solidify a College Football Playoff spot. Bishop, a Heisman Trophy candidate and Doak Walker Award finalist, suffered a lower-body injury in a 27-13 win over LSU on Nov. 21. He left the game and did not return. Bishop, a former Karns High standout, leads the SEC in rushing with 1,215 yards along with 13 touchdowns. His 248 rushing attempts are second most in the nation. Carter, a former Smyrna High standout, suffered a lower leg injury in a 27-13 win over LSU on Nov. 21. He leads the team with 76 tackles, along with 11 tackles-for-loss, five sacks and three fumble recoveries. Eleven Tennessee players have suffered season-ending injuries in 2026: starting wide receiver Mike Matthews (knee); starting guard Nic Moore (undisclosed medical condition); starting defensive end Tyree Weathersby (knee); starting guard Wendell Moe (lower leg); starting safety Edrees Farooq (knee); starting tight end Ethan Davis (knee); running back Daune Morris (broken leg); safety Dylan Lewis (foot); wide receiver/kick returner Joakim Dodson (leg); linebacker Jaedon Harmon (knee); and cornerback Jadais Richard (upper-body). Tennessee football injury report LB Arion Carter (questionable, lower leg) RB DeSean Bishop (questionable, lower body) OL Nic Moore (out for season, undisclosed medical condition) WR Mike Matthews (out for season, knee) RB Daune Morris (out for season, broken leg) DE Tyree Weathersby (out for season, knee) OL Wendell Moe (out for season, lower leg) DB Dylan Lewis (out for season, foot) S Edrees Farooq (out for season, knee) TE Ethan Davis (out for season, knee) KR/WR Joakim Dodson (out for season, leg) LB Jaedon Harmon (out for season, knee) CB Jadais Richard (out for season, upper-body) Vanderbilt football injury report OL Clinton Azubuike (questionable) CB Cobey Sellers (out) QB Blaze Berlowitz (out) DL Edwin Kolenge (out) LB Josiah Broxton (out) RB Evan Hampton (out) LB Daniel Vollmer Jr. (out) OL Gunner Givens (out) DL Aaron Bryant (out) How SEC availability report works The SEC student-athlete availability report was introduced in the 2024 season for conference games only. The initial report is released on Wednesday of an SEC game week, with daily updates leading to a final report 90 minutes prior to kickoff of a Saturday game. Prior to game day, players are designated by their school as available, probable, questionable, doubtful or out for the upcoming game. On game day, they are designated as available, game-time decision or out. Here’s what those designations mean: • Out: Will not play, 0% chance to play. • Doubtful: Unlikely to play, 25% chance to play. • Questionable: Uncertain to play, 50% chance to play. • Probable: Probable to play, 75% chance to play. Per SEC policy, schools must accurately designate players’ participation status. If the school has knowledge that a player may not be able to participate in the upcoming game for any reason (injury, illness, suspension, ineligibility or personal matter), it must report it. Failure to do so will subject schools to potential penalties ranging from $25,000 for a first offense to $100,000 for a third and further offenses.
