title: Meet IndyStar motorsports reporter Zion Brown
summary: Meet IndyStar journalists who bring you the news from around Central Indiana. Up this week is Zion Brown
content: It takes a staff of dedicated journalists to bring you the news from around Central Indiana. In this feature, the Indianapolis Star introduces readers to our newsroom staff — or, rather, we let them introduce themselves. Up this week is Zion Brown. What's your job title? Motorsports reporter When did you join IndyStar? I joined IndyStar in January 2026. I previously interned at IndyStar in 2023 and 2024. What's your favorite part of your job? My favorite part of my job is the vastness of the stories I get to tell. IndyCar is my main focus, and that gives me dozens of drivers and 11 full-time teams that I can focus on. At the same time, I get to tell stories from other series like NASCAR, NHRA and IMSA. There are hardly ever dull weeks on this beat, especially in season. Why journalism? I chose journalism because I've always been observant and curious. I believe those skills come before getting into the technicalities of writing stories. In sports, stories give the action further meaning, which is what I always aim to accomplish in my work. People don't just want to know what happened – they want to know why it matters. What's your favorite Indy area restaurant or hidden gem? Famous Steak & Lemonade is wonderful. Don't let the title fool you, as the chicken is probably the draw of the restaurant. What do you do to unwind from a job that can be stressful? I typically go on walks or read to unwind. What are you reading or streaming? I am currently reading Preston Lerner's "The Deadliest Decade," a book about the technological advances that led to more deaths in racing from 1964 to 1973, and the safety measures that came during and after this period. What’s the best piece of advice you ever received? How you do anything is how you do everything. If you could guest star on any TV show past or present, which one? I'd love to have a guest role on "Atlanta." Do you prefer dogs or cats? I'm allergic to many dogs, and still believe they're the superior pet. What's the meanest tweet ever directed at you? After one article I wrote this year, someone suggested that I have fewer brain cells than red pandas – which have one brain cell. I'm not sure if that was really the meanest insult ever directed at me, but it was certainly the most clever. What's your bucket-list vacation destination? I'd love to visit Hawaii. I'll give an honorable mention to Australia as well. Zion Brown is IndyStar's motorsports reporter. Follow him at @z10nbr0wn . title: Alabama basketball freshmen take step forward in Las Vegas vs Kansas State
summary: Alabama basketball bounced back against Kansas State with the help of its freshmen. How the rookies gained Nate Oats' trust in Vegas.
content: Alabama basketball rediscovered its offensive rhythm in Las Vegas, although putting Kansas State away proved more difficult than building a comfortable lead. After dropping its Players Era Festival opener to Baylor, the Crimson Tide bounced back with a 104-91 victory over Kansas State on Thursday, Nov. 26, at T-Mobile Arena. Here are three takeaways from No. 15 Alabama 's Thanksgiving win. IN THE PROS: Alabama basketball alum Labaron Philon puts NBA on notice, earns praise from LeBron James RECAP, HIGHLIGHTS: Alabama basketball holds off Kansas State in Vegas Qayden Samuels making case for Nate Oats to keep him on the floor After Kansas State (3-4) took its first lead of the night, Samuels needed just 27 seconds to knock down consecutive 3-pointers and put Alabama (6-1) back in front. As valuable as the non-starter's perimeter shooting was, his ability to stay involved when shots weren't coming his way was just as important. Samuels needed seven first-half minutes to score 12 points and finished with a team-high 14 on just three field-goal attempts, converting all eight of his free throws while grabbing six boards on the night. "That's about as efficient as you can get," Oats said. Although five turnovers illustrated where there's still room for growth, Samuels was among four freshmen Oats trusted to help close out the game and three who finished with double figures. "I wanted to keep some of the veteran guys' minutes down," Oats said. Amari Allen, Aden Holloway prove stability Crimson Tide needs early There were moments when it seemed like Alabama could use Allen or Holloway to take over the game, and while the offense eventually found its footing, it may not have if not for its most experienced ball-handlers. Allen got bigs involved early, finding Kentucky transfer Brandon Garrison for two baskets before setting up Boise State transfer Drew Fielder for a dunk. Later, Holloway helped NC State transfer freshman Cole Cloer find his rhythm from beyond the arc, assisting on a pair of 3-pointers in a 29-second span. Despite combining for just 11 points themselves, the returning duo accounted for 10 of Alabama's 12 first-half assists. Their willingness to share the ball helped seven Crimson Tide players reach double digits and gave Oats the luxury of subbing out Allen with four minutes to play and Holloway with 9 1/2 minutes remaining ahead of Friday's meeting with Miami. Alabama still learning how to put teams away As encouraged as Oats was by Alabama's defensive effort against Baylor, Thursday showed how easily the Crimson Tide can undermine its own progress. Kansas State shot just 33% from the field in the second half but still managed to score 56 points. Alabama's 21 turnovers yielded 20 points for the Wildcats. Even when the Crimson Tide forced missed shots, Kansas State extended possessions by grabbing 13 offensive rebounds in the second half and generating 15 second-chance points. Factor in the Wildcats' 24 made free throws after halftime, and it's easier to understand why Oats came away encouraged by Alabama's defense itself, although frustrated with its discipline. "If we clean those up, I thought we had an outstanding game defensively," Oats said. Emilee Smarr covers Alabama basketball and Crimson Tide athletics for The Tuscaloosa News. She can be reached via email at esmarr@usatodayco.com. This article originally appeared on The Tuscaloosa News: Alabama basketball freshmen take step forward in Las Vegas vs Kansas State

title: Arkansas basketball loses to Michigan State but makes progress
summary: Arkansas didn't get a quality win, but the Hogs seemed to grow up
content: Arkansas basketball lost another game to a power conference opponent on Thursday. The Razorbacks dropped a 70-67 thriller to Michigan State in Detroit. The end result isn't good, but to be quite honest, this was a real step forward for John Calipari's team. It's absolutely true that moral victories are not the point of competition , and that a team with Sweet 16 and maybe Elite Eight potential is still behind schedule for the season, given the lack of high-end wins on its resume. However, given how bad this team looked against Virginia and Indiana, the performance against Tom Izzo's team should be encouraging for John Calipari and his staff. It no longer seems that Arkansas is hopelessly and substantially lost as a team. The defense was a lot better against Michigan State than it was against Indiana. This team needs to be good at the defensive end of the floor in order to be a real contender in the SEC, and the defensive performance on Thanksgiving moves the needle several notches in the right direction. Arkansas forced 13 Michigan State turnovers and blocked 5 shots. Michigan State did shoot over 50 percent, but it wasn't as though the Spartans were getting to the rim with regularity. Michigan State shot the cover off the ball from 3-point range, going 8 of 12. Most opponents aren't going to shoot that well with such a small sample size. Arkansas' effort in this game was excellent. The Hogs collected 17 offensive rebounds to just 7 for Michigan State. Arkansas began to look like the hungry team we hoped it would be before the season began. Michigan State prides itself on hustle and toughness. Arkansas matched Michigan State in that regard, a big sign of growth and evolution for the young Razorbacks. John Calipari really seemed to get through to his young guys on the need to play every possession with passion and forget the previous play. Arkansas was more mature and more forwardly-focused in this game. The players are beginning to understand what it takes to win... but they're not quite there. As good as the effort was for Arkansas, the inability to finish plays is hugely frustrating for the Razorbacks. They hit just 3 of 23 3-point shots. They made only 10 of 16 free throws. Jeremiah Wilkinson and Billy Richmond were a combined 1 for 14 on threes. Arkansas gained Wilkinson in the transfer portal specifically for his offense. As we have said before, if Wilkinson isn't making shots, he's a net negative for this team. Arkansas - which seemed like a deep team on paper before the season began - got just 2 points and 5 rebounds from its bench in 36 total minutes. Arkansas doesn't have the eight- or nine-deep rotation which was supposed to wear down opponents with smothering, constant energy. The better overall performance against Michigan State came from the discovery of the best starting five so far this season, with Davion Thompson starting and Miikka Muurinen going to the bench, two moves we thought Calipari needed to make. The starting five appears to be set, but now the bench needs to give Arkansas a lot more production. The Hogs improved, but now they need to finish off important games against high-quality opponents. It's time to start building an NCAA Tournament resume. Arkansas isn't in a state of full-blown crisis, but the Razorbacks have to start winning the most significant games on their schedule. They can't continue to swing and miss as December arrives.

title: Chauncey Wiggins Let It Fly in Gonzaga’s 72-64 Victory Over Baylor
summary: Two Jesuit institutions face off in the Players Era 16's T-Mobile Arena bracket final: Creighton and Gonzaga.
content: LAS VEGAS, NEVADA - NOVEMBER 26: Chauncey Wiggins #9 and Braden Huff #34 of the Gonzaga Bulldogs wave as they leave the court after the team's 72-64 victory over the Baylor Bears in a semifinal game of the Players Era 16 tournament at T-Mobile Arena on November 26, 2026 in Las Vegas, Nevada. (Photo by Ethan Miller/Getty Images) | Getty Images With an embarrassingly low-attendance semifinal matchup at the T-Mobile Arena in Las Vegas, Nevada, the No. 22 Gonzaga Bulldogs (5-1 Pac-12 Conference) sought more revenge against the Baylor Bears (5-2 Big 12 Conference) after the disappointing 2021 national championship loss. Unfortunately, it was hard to watch with all the court advertisements and unnecessary sky camera shots from the ESPN crew in another late night at the Players Era 16. Star sophomore wing Davis Fogle struggled to find any type of rhythm for coach Mark Few, only ending up with four points on 1-for-7 overall shooting in 29 minutes of play. The Zags had multiple bench pieces replace that missing production from the team’s leading offensive threat after outscoring coach Scott Drew’s reserves 38-28. In the first half, it was the fast pace under starting fifth-year point guard Xaivian Lee and fifth-year point guard Nathan De Sousa in the second unit that truly opened up the floor for everyone else. Specifically for fifth-year forward Chauncey Wiggins, who kept his headband on for the full contest this time, and junior forward/center Izan Almansa. Almansa had a perfect performance with 11 points on 5-for-5 field goals/1-for-1 three-pointers, quickly becoming one of the most reliable and physical depth pieces on the roster. It was raining three-pointers for Wiggins, who finished with a team-high 19 points on 7-for-11 shooting from the field/5-7 from beyond the arc, to go along with six rebounds, three assists, and two steals. An unconditional push shot, but the 6-10 sniper with the quick release has been consistent throughout his collegiate career with the Clemson Tigers and Florida State Seminoles. Wiggins is someone to lean on when buckets are tough to come by, as was evident in the first half against a feisty bunch of Bears. Expect to see Drew’s bunch in the AP Top 25 poll come Monday, Nov. 30. As for an experienced De Sousa, the Frenchman completely understands his role: finding open scorers, not turning it over or taking bad shots, while embracing being a pest as an on-ball defender. He will only be with the Pacific Northwest program for one campaign, but wants to make the most of every single one of his minutes out there. A winning impact. Baylor’s brotherly backcourt, freshman guard Dylan Mingo and sophomore guard Kayden Mingo, were kept at bay for the majority of this high-level competition. But Gonzaga was just much too confident a group when stretching out the floor. They would go 8-for-14 in the first half, putting themselves in the driver’s seat the rest of the way. This was Gonzaga’s best win to date, now prepping for a quick turnaround with theCreighton Bluejays (6-1 Big East Conference) in the T-Mobile Arena’s bracket final on Friday, Nov. 27, viewable on ESPN at 8:00 p.m. PT. This will be a sneak preview before the second non-conference opportunity between the two Jesuit institutions, when the Zags head to the CHI Health Center in Omaha, Nebraska, to take on the Bluejays on Dec. 12. In their 95-87 semifinal victory against the TCU Horned Frogs earlier in the day, four of five Creighton starters totaled in double digits, led by senior guard Wes Enis with 20 points in 34 minutes of action for first-year coach Alan Huss. The Bluejays hit 11 three-pointers on 26 attempts (42.3 percent) over the Horned Frogs. Creighton’s offense has been on a roll in their last two outings in Sin City, scoring 194 points in their triumphs over last season’s national champion Michigan Wolverines in the quarterfinals and TCU. Whoever can earn the most three-pointers and guard the perimeter with a purpose will book their trip to Saturday, Nov. 28’s championship game. Does Few’s unit have enough in the tank to win two more games in two days and come away with an additional $300,000 on top of its baseline Name, Image, and Likeness (NIL) compensation from the tournament, which would add up to over $1 million? The closing of halves continues to be a glaring issue for Gonzaga, not crashing the defensive glass enough (especially when sophomore center Massamba Diop is looking from the sidelines/in foul trouble) and releasing their foot off the gas pedal heading into the conclusions of both first- and second-half locker rooms. title: Everything you need to know as Notre Dame basketball hosts Stonehill
summary: Notre Dame basketball has been good to start the regular season, but there remains plenty of non-conference home work as December nears
content: SOUTH BEND – So, this is what it's like to be at home to play some hoops over Thanksgiving weekend holiday for Notre Dame basketball. It's been a minute since the Irish have done both. This game marks the first time since 2018 that Notre Dame will play at home for Thanksgiving weekend. No multi-team event somewhere warmer. No break from an earlier MTE somewhere nicer. The Irish wrap two home games over the holiday week with their first Saturday game on Thanksgiving weekend since a 95-70 win over DePaul at Purcell Pavilion on Nov. 24, 2018. Noie: For this Notre Dame basketball program this season, talk is not cheap Noie: That Notre Dame basketball bandwagon is about to get a bit crowded Another chance for Notre Dame to be better, to get better, as the calendar crawls toward league play. Notre Dame basketball versus Stonehill Date: Saturday, November 28 Start time: 8 p.m. Site: Purcell Pavilion (9,149) Tickets: Available. What channel is Notre Dame basketball versus Stonehill on? Streaming : ACCNX Radio : 960 WSBT-AM in South Bend. Also on SiriusXM on ACC Radio and channels 955 and 956. You can also listen live free on Audacy. Live streaming: https://www.fubo.tv/stream/tv/? Series history between Notre Dame basketball and Stonehill Notre Dame leads 3-0 with all three meetings in South Bend – 1977, 1982 and the opener for the 2024-25 season on Nov. 6, 2024. Markus Burton led the Irish with 18 points, three rebounds and five assists. Braeden Shrewsberry had 18 points, four rebounds and one assist. Matt Allocco added 10 points, three rebounds and two assists for the Irish, who led for 37:05 and by as many as 29. Notre Dame scored 32 points in the paint and had 25 bench points in the first of four wins to start the season. Notre Dame basketball versus Stonehill storylines ∎ Notre Dame opened this week 6-1 with Stonehill 2-4. Both played games on Tuesday – Notre Dame at home against Central Michigan and Stonehill at home against Vermont State – prior to Tribune print deadlines heading into this game. ∎ Irish point guard Braeden Smith opened the week ranked third in the ACC in assists (6.29) and assist/turnover ratio (3.38) and fifth for steals (2.43). In three games in Las Vegas, Smith averaged 17.6 points, 5.6 rebounds and 5.0 assists in 32.6 minutes. ∎ After finishing the last three seasons at Nos. 269, 261 and 335 nationally for assist/turnover ratio, Notre Dame ranked No. 90 (361 schools) after seven games with a 1.47 A/T ratio. ∎ The Irish entered the final full week of November ranked first in the ACC and second in the nation for 3-point field goal percentage (45.4) trailing only UC Santa Barbara (46.2). Sophomore Brady Koehler was tops in the ACC at .645 (20-for-31). ∎ Located in North Easton, Massachusetts, Stonehill made the move to full-fledge Division I membership on June 24, 2025. This is the final season of competition as a member of the Northeast Conference. On July 1, 2027, Stonehill will move to the Metro Conference. ∎ Former Irish basketball manager Brendan Sullivan (a 2001 Notre Dame graduate) served as Stonehill athletics director from 2008-15. He also worked in athletics administration at Holy Cross and Boston University. Sullivan is now chief financial officer at The Newman School in Boston. ∎ One of four Northeast Conference schools on Notre Dame's non-league schedule this season, Stonehill returned one starter off a team that finished 12-21 overall, 8-10 and tied for sixth in the NEC last season. The Skyhawks were picked this preseason to finish sixth in the nine-team NEC. Keep an eye on ... Stonehill G Anquan Boldin, Jr. (4) Five games as the energy guy off the bench were enough for the 6-foot-4 senior transfer from Delray Beach, Florida, who averaged 5.8 points and 3.0 rebounds last season at Florida A&M. Like his former NFL standout wide receiver father who made a living going over the middle and delivering, Bouldin is a slasher who goes down the lane and finishes at the rim. He made his first start last week against Northeastern, a 95-82 Stonehill win, and had 10 points with two rebounds. Heading into this week, Bouldin was averaging 8.7 points on an offensively challenged team (67.3 ppg.) with 3.5 rebounds and 0.5 assists in 23.5 minutes. He was shooting .667 percent from the field, .750 from 3 and .591 from the foul line. Bouldin's top fun fact from his bio on the Stonehill web page? He's been to over 20 countries. Notre Dame PF Bryce Ruglass-Dortch (4) Three games in Las Vegas at the Players Era 8 tournament were a trial by fire for the 6-foot-9, 235-pound Ruglass-Dortch as the Irish scramble to find a serviceable backup big for Logan Duncomb while sophomore Tommy Ahneman recovers from a right arm (wrist) injury suffered earlier this season. Asking Ruglass-Dortch, a Rutgers transfer, to fit seamlessly into the rotation against the likes of Florida and Auburn was a big ask. Ruglass-Dortch looked overmatched at times, but in others, looked like he fits. Like when he got loose in the paint late against Rutgers, but instead of forcing it, kicked to Koehler for an open 3 in the corner to put the Irish up 3. It was a small play, but a big basketball play. At 1.3 points and 2.0 rebounds in 11.7 minutes the first seven games, Ruglass-Dortch may not ever score it or rebound it like a main guy, but if he can offer quality backup minutes, that's a start for someone still scratching the surface as to who he might be over these next two seasons. This is a big non-league stretch for him to build confidence for conference play. title: Highlights: MSU basketball dominates second half, tops Arkansas on Thanksgiving
summary: Watch highlights from the Spartans' dominant second half performance to top Arkansas on Thanksgiving in the Motor City
content: Michigan State basketball was a turkey day winner -- but it wasn't easy by any means. The Spartans used a dominant second half performance to rally to a 70-67 victory over Arkansas from the Little Caesars Arena in Detroit on Thanksgiving. The Spartans trailed for a good chunk of the game. But a 24-2 run in the second half gave them the edge that was good enough to pull out the win. Luckily for Michigan State, poor free throw shooting in the final minute didn't haunt them, as a last second three-point attempt from Arkansas bounced out to seal the victory. Michigan State was led by All-American Jeremy Fears Jr., who finished with a double-double at 20 points and 10 assists. Jordan Scott also was a key factor in the win, providing stellar defense and 15 points. The Spartans improve to 6-1 on the year with the win over Arkansas. Michigan State will next play Minnesota on Wednesday. content: Nov. 27—BEMIDJI — Jaxon Boschee ended his Bemidji High School basketball career as the highest-scoring player in school history, and he had a decision to make. Where's the best place for him to play in college? An obvious candidate was Bemidji State, where his dad, Mike Boschee, has been the head coach since 2012. But Jaxon had other offers, such as Florida Tech, Northern Michigan and the NSIC's Minot State. "I think they always thought that if he was going to go D-II, it probably would have been Bemidji State," Mike said. Jaxon could've had a fresh start in another town, but he decided to stay home. In March, he committed to play for the Beavers. He made his collegiate debut on Nov. 13, when BSU tipped off the season against Northwest Missouri State at the Hillyard Tipoff Classic. Coming off the bench, he put up 11 points, grabbed two rebounds and had two assists. For a freshman making his debut in the first game of the season, it was an impressive performance. Four games later, Jaxon had found himself in the starting lineup against Minnesota Duluth. He tied for a team-high 14 points, shooting 50% from the field. "It's not easy for any freshman on any college team to come in and help," Mike said. "But he's doing a nice job; he's fitting in really well. He's playing solid basketball. Obviously, he has a lot of room to grow and to get over some of the freshman things that all freshmen do, but now he's doing well." Jaxon's first home game against Concordia College on Nov. 17 was made even more special when his name was called during the reading of the starting lineups for the first time. As a freshman, it wasn't something he necessarily expected that early into his career. "It wasn't my main focus," Jaxon said. "I was more just process-driven and sticking to my routine and whatever happens, happens. And if I get an opportunity, I make the most of it." In a three-game homestand against Valley City State, UMD and Concordia College, Jaxon averaged 30 minutes a game and started all three games. His strong play earned his way into the starting lineup, according to Mike. "I think there's always a good chunk— maybe eight to 15 freshmen in our conference — that are out there playing (significant minutes)," he said. "He's certainly one of those guys that's earned that, and it's a credit to him and his work ethic." Growing up, Mike coached Jaxon when he was playing in Bemidji's youth basketball system, so being together at the D-II level hasn't come with many adjustments for the father-son duo. "There's kind of a flip that gets switched between dad and coach," Jaxon said. "You just have to know the difference of when it's coach talking and when it's dad talking." Mike added: "It's really not what people think, like, you're coaching your kid out there. It's more that I'm coaching a basketball player that's part of our team." While Jaxon has had some early success, it's come with some typical freshman learning experiences. It's a natural process when shifting from playing the regular Section 8-4A schools for Bemidji High School to playing against the best the NSIC has to offer. "The biggest thing for me is just the physicality and the speed of it," Jaxon said. "There aren't too many small players out here, so you have to really be sharp with your ball handling and getting your shots off quick." He's been adjusting to the level of play well, Mike said. He particularly kept his strong 3-point shooting that made him such a dangerous player at BHS. Jaxon isn't the only former Lumberjack on the Beavers. Senior Isaac Severts was a teammate of Jaxon's at BHS before graduating in 2023. He has helped guide Jaxon's transition to the collegiate level. Jaxon has also leaned on seniors like Tate Olson and John Pecarich, who commonly find themselves on top of the stat sheet for BSU. After making so much history at the BHS Gymnasium, fans can still watch the local kid representing the city well. And who knows, maybe Jaxon can make a run at the Bemidji State points record, too.

title: King Rice opens up on absence from UNC basketball, emotional return | Exclusive
summary: The UNC basketball vs. Monmouth score was forgettable for King Rice. The moments shared with longtime mentors, teammates and friends were not.
content: CHAPEL HILL — The emotions didn’t fully hit King Rice until he returned to the visiting locker room at the Smith Center following a 40-point loss to his alma mater. Rice, 57, certainly wasn’t pleased with Monmouth’s performance in an 85-45 defeat to North Carolina . But after nearly 500 games as the Hawks’ head coach over 16 seasons, he knows wins and losses come and go. What lingered was bigger than results. More than 40 years of memories and relationships came flooding back when Rice saw who was waiting for him after the game. MALONE'S PATH: Michael Malone goes from practice ejection to lifelong loyalty at Seton Hall Prep | Exclusive UNC BASKETBALL REUNION: The moment at UNC's basketball reunion that caught Michael Malone off guard Former UNC guard Kenny Smith was there. So were former Tar Heels assistant coaches Phil Ford and Dave Hanners. Dave Blaha, a former walk-on who often gave Rice rides home to upstate New York during their playing days, was there too. Rice hadn’t seen Blaha since the 1990s. “That’s when it got emotional for me,” Rice said during a 20-minute conversation with The Fayetteville Observer. “Because I didn’t play with Kenny. Obviously, Coach Ford coached me and helped me grow up a whole bunch. But then Coach Hanners came in there and said, ‘Listen to this guy. He cares about y’all, he loves y’all. I know he yells and uses curse words sometimes, but he’s trying to get y’all to do the right things. It’s all from the right place.’ ” It was a special moment because, as Rice mentioned, "those guys are Carolina men and they came to support me" at the Smith Center. “They know I don’t like losing like that. They know that crushed everything in my being, but you got to be a man, you got to stand up. This isn’t the first time I’ve gotten my butt kicked, it’s not going to be the last time I get my butt kicked," Rice said. “But, as a man, you got to stand up. Your friends are still there for you. Even though I didn’t play with those guys, they came to support and that’s where my kids can learn the most from. It’s bigger than basketball. Yeah, we got whupped (Monday), but it’s bigger than basketball and the experience was great for us. We’ll be better because of how that game went.” A loss is temporary. Family is forever. Why King Rice stayed away, eventually returned to UNC A four-year player for Dean Smith and the Tar Heels from 1987-91, Rice scored 861 points, dished out 629 assists and racked up 147 steals. He helped the program win two ACC Tournament championships and, as a captain in 1991, made the Final Four. Even after a long absence — including 10 years between games in Chapel Hill — and what Rice described as “some hurt feelings,” he returned to Chapel Hill for a UNC basketball reunion in October before Monmouth’s Nov. 23 game against the Tar Heels. UNC hosted Monmouth in 2012 and 2016 under Roy Williams, but Rice said he hadn’t been back to the Smith Center in a “long time” before he attended the reunion with his wife and two sons. “That was cool for them just to be there with me,” Rice said. “When you haven’t been back for so long, you put your guard up. So my guard’s been up and it was cool that I could put it down.” So what happened to keep Rice away from Chapel Hill for so long? “The things that went on, things happened. My feelings got hurt,” Rice said. “Coach Williams, before he retired, they were getting ready to come and play at Monmouth, which was going to be a huge deal for my university, for me, for all of us. That got canceled. Coach Williams was calling me apologizing and saying sorry.” Rice never lost contact with Williams, but things clearly weren't the same during the Hubert Davis era, which started in 2021 and ended earlier this year. “Coach Williams has been A1 with me. I think he felt bad that I wasn’t coming back to Chapel Hill for a while, but he and I stayed in touch. He was really the only one that I really stayed in touch with. Now, we’re just moving forward,” Rice said. “I never wanted anything bad for Hubert. I know his wife, his kids, so I wanted Hubert to be the coach there for 100 years. It didn’t go that way and now Michael’s the coach. Michael’s really working on the Carolina basketball family for all of us, so it can be forever again. And that is needed. Families need work. You have to work on families.” For Rice, staying connected was easier when Dean Smith and Williams served as the program’s patriarchs. Together, they spent 54 seasons as UNC’s head coaches. With Malone arriving as the first outsider to be hired at UNC since Frank McGuire in 1952, the first-year coach has made a concerted effort to re-emphasize the important of the program's history by connecting with people who helped make the blue blood program what it is today. “We were raised on Coach Smith reaching out. We were raised on Coach Guthridge reaching out, knowing your kids’ names and saying hello to your mom and still sending your parents Christmas cards," Rice said. "That’s Carolina basketball. That’s why we’re different than any other family. But you still have to work on your family to make sure grandma and grandpa are good, Uncle Jimmy’s good, you got to make sure everybody’s good. I’m glad that they thought it was important to include me in that.” King Rice, Dean Smith and the Carolina family Rice is candid about his past, using his mistakes to shape how he coaches and deals with his current players. He isn’t willing to give up on them because Smith never gave up on him. “I do a lot of the things that I do because of what Coach Smith did with me,” said Rice, who wore a “DES” pin for the UNC game. “I was a kid and I made some poor choices. Coach Smith always remembered that I was a kid and everybody else was like, ‘He’s messing up, he’s this and that.’ ” Rice said Smith continued believing in him as he struggled with alcoholism, convincing Rice that it wasn't all about what he could do as a player at UNC. Smith wanted Rice to be the person he knew he was capable of becoming. “I was a kid from upstate New York that got to come to North Carolina and was going to change the world, and the ride became a little bumpy for me,” Rice said. “Coach Smith kept believing in me and I kept plugging. When I realized I had a drinking problem, a real severe one, Coach Smith was trying to explain that to me when I was a kid. But I was a kid and wouldn’t listen. “Then I was 27 years old and said, ‘Maybe he was right. Maybe my mom and everyone telling me was right and I do have this problem.’ I haven’t had a drink since then. Nobody’s heard any crazy King stories since I quit drinking 30 years ago. … Because Coach Smith believed in me and he kept believing in me, now I am a head coach and been doing it for 16 years. The problem kid turned into the head coach that has 45 graduates under his name.” Rice, along with assistant coaches and fellow former Tar Heel guards Brian Reese and Shammond Williams, received applause from the Smith Center crowd before Monmouth’s game. Reese said "it's always nice to be back home," but admitted this time was even more special because of Rice's return after the long break. In addition to Ford, Hanners and Kenny Smith, Rasheed Wallace, JR Reid, Jimmy Black, Luke Maye, Quentin Thomas and Warren Martin – who scored the first basket in the Smith Center – were among the other Tar Heels in attendance. And Williams , who brought Rice back to Chapel Hill during the 2005-06 season as a volunteer assistant, was waiting outside of the tunnel to greet Monmouth's head coach before the game. They shared a hug, said they loved each other and Rice embraced Kenny Smith as he walked toward the Hawks' bench. Following the Marshall game, Malone mentioned Rice's impending return during his postgame news conference. "I'm excited to welcome King Rice back," Malone said. "I think it's going to be really great to have King back, such a storied player in this tradition of this great program. So I'm thankful that King is coming back." Legends in the building on Monday night. Head coach King Rice with Roy Williams and Kenny Smith. #FlyHawks pic.twitter.com/8O6hH1Efy1 — Monmouth Basketball (@MonmouthBBall) November 24, 2026 It was a reunion that needed to happen and one that allowed Rice’s family – his wife, Summer, and their two sons, Xander and Julian James – the chance to reunite with his other family. “When my feelings got hurt and I wasn’t coming back, my family didn’t come back,” Rice said. “Both of my sons, my older son was like, ‘Dad, I’m not mad with them. I’d always go back to Chapel Hill.’ My wife went there, too, so she’d always want to go back. And my little guy, he hadn’t been there since he was 3 or 4 years old. To me, once I calmed down and could see past the emotions of it at first, I was cheating my family from a major part in me and my wife’s relationship by not going back down there.” Rice credited Sean May, Pat Sullivan, Eric Hoots and Malone for helping re-establish those connections, reminding him that there's no expiration date once you're a part of the UNC family. “That’s what Carolina basketball’s all about. I got told, Shammond got told, Brian got told, every player got told that this is forever. This is what makes us different. This is forever,” Rice said. “Nobody told us, ‘Oh, King, this is for when you’re here. And when Coach Smith isn’t here anymore, it’s over.’ No one ever said that. Carolina basketball, if you come here, is forever. That’s how it felt this time. So I’m honored that I got to bring my team. I’m thankful. I’m thankful to Michael, I’m thankful to Sean, I’m thankful to Pat, I’m thankful to Hoots. Those guys have been friends for a long time and they thought it would mean enough to me and the former guys to bring my team back after we weren’t back for a while. That was a really good deal.” King Rice gets a Carolina welcome during introductions. #FlyHawks pic.twitter.com/8xtr52Vmca — Monmouth Basketball (@MonmouthBBall) November 24, 2026 Whether it’s one year or 10 years, there’s something about coming home that makes everything feel OK. Even after a 40-point loss, the relationships were strong enough to put basketball in perspective. That bond, Rice reiterated, “means everything to my family.” It’s also something he hopes his younger son gets to experience someday. “I never quit, I kept growing and now they call me head coach,” Rice said. “I’ve got a son that graduated from Bucknell, my other son is an A-student – he’s so bright, UNC should be getting him just for academics. Hopefully, he’s going to keep getting better and another Rice will have a chance to play basketball there and do it a different way than his daddy did.” Rodd Baxley covers North Carolina Tar Heels athletics for The Fayetteville Observer as part of the USA TODAY Network. Follow his ACC coverage on X/Twitter or Bluesky: @RoddBaxley. Got questions regarding UNC? Send them to rbaxley@usatodayco.com . title: Live score updates, highlights for Alabama basketball vs Miami in Players Era
summary: Before going to Coral Gables next week, Alabama basketball meets Miami in the Players Era Festival. Live score updates, highlights from Vegas.
content: Alabama basketball is getting an early look at an opponent it was already preparing to face in December. The No. 15 Crimson Tide (6-1) will conclude its time at the Players Era Festival against No. 17 Miami (6-2) on Friday, Nov. 27, at T-Mobile Arena in Las Vegas. The teams will battle for fifth place in their tournament bracket before meeting again in the ACC/SEC Challenge. Both are coming off Thanksgiving victories after suffering losses to unranked opponents in the opening round. Alabama defeated Kansas State 104-91 after falling to Baylor, while Miami rebounded from a loss to TCU with a 97-70 rout of reigning national champion Michigan. Although Alabama's freshmen showed encouraging signs of growth against the Wildcats, turnovers and defensive rebounding remain priorities for coach Nate Oats as the Crimson Tide looks to secure its first ranked win of the season. Follow along for live score updates, highlights and more from Alabama's Players Era Festival finale. WHAT TO KNOW: What we know about Tarris Bouie's absence for Alabama basketball in Las Vegas REQUIRED READING: Alabama basketball freshmen take step forward in Las Vegas vs Kansas State Alabama basketball vs Miami series history Alabama holds a 3-1 advantage in the all-time series against Miami, which dates back to December 1968. Friday marks the first meeting between the programs since Nov. 28, 2021, when Oats led Alabama to a 96-64 victory over the Hurricanes in the ESPN Events Invitational in Orlando, Florida. Miami's lone victory over Alabama came in the second round of the 2015 NIT, when the Hurricanes defeated the Crimson Tide 73-66 in Coral Gables. When does Alabama basketball play Miami again in the ACC/SEC Challenge? Alabama will travel to Coral Gables for a rematch against Miami on Wednesday, Dec. 2, at the Watsco Center. Tipoff is scheduled for 8:15 p.m. CT on ESPN. Alabama is 2-1 in the ACC/SEC Challenge since its inception in 2023, having won its last two matchups against North Carolina and Clemson. title: Louisville basketball on exorcism tour at Players Era 16. Up next? UT
summary: Louisville basketball is on an exorcism tour at the Players Era 16. Up next for Pat Kelsey's Cardinals? A chance to make history vs. Tennessee.
content: LAS VEGAS — Pat Kelsey is on one hell of an exorcism tour in Sin City. Louisville basketball hasn't beaten an AP top-five team under his watch? Done . Living in the lingering shadow of Rick Pitino ? He just took down the Hall of Famer in an instant classic — decided by a buzzer-beating 3-pointer from Adrian Wooley . What's next? Funny you should ask. It's the team that doled out the first butt-kicking of his tenure. And did it again last season . We're talking, of course, about No. 11 Tennessee (7-0). The 23rd-ranked Cardinals (5-1) and the Rick Barnes' Volunteers are set for a 9 p.m. tipoff Nov. 27 at Michelob ULTRA Arena — with a spot in the Players Era 16 championship game on the line. UofL hasn't played three consecutive games against teams ranked in the AP Top 25 since February 2019. According to a post from statistician Kelly Dickey on X, formerly Twitter , the program has never notched three straight wins over AP top-15 opponents. If that's going to happen, Louisville must embrace a third street fight in four days on less than 24 hours' rest. "When you play coach Barnes' team, it's going to be (a) bare-knuckles backyard brawl," Kelsey said after the Cards beat the Red Storm. "We've got to be ready to answer that physical challenge." That wasn't the case in either UofL-UT matchup the past two seasons. Tennessee combined to outrebound Louisville 75-56. It also combined to outscore the Cards 82-40 in the paint and held them to 38-for-118 (32.2%) shooting. This isn't the same UofL, though. Kelsey's intentional approach to address the red flags raised during those games has paid off to this point of the 2026-27 campaign. "The good news for us is: We have a tough, physical group of dudes, too," the coach said after his team improved its Players Era 16 rebounding margin to +16 by outworking St. John's on the glass — to the tune of an 18-8 edge in second-chance scoring. Entering the matchup with the Vols , KenPom.com ranked Louisville sixth nationally in offensive rebounding rate. The Cards have corralled 44.1% of their missed shots — up from 32.8% in 2025-26. Six players were averaging 4.2 boards or more per game. Junior forward Flory Bidunga leads the way with 9.2. "He is a stone-cold killer around the basket," Kelsey said. UofL also has a bruising guard on a heater: fifth-year transfer Seth Trimble , who went for a career-high 33 points on 12-for-19 shooting in 32 minutes off the bench vs. the Red Storm. Afterward, Pitino said the 6-foot-3 Wisconsin native is "as tough of a guard going to the basket as there is in the country." But ... "But your reputation doesn't mean you're going to be great at that tomorrow," Kelsey said. "We've got to play hard; we've got to play physical." As of Nov. 27, UT boasted the country's fourth-best scoring defense, allowing only 57.5 points per game, and ranked No. 1 in field-goal percentage defense (27.8%, including a 20.6% from beyond the arc). Its rebounding numbers aren't great, however: 175th in margin, 303rd in offensive boards per contest. It all comes down to this. "Who can be resilient?" Kelsey said. title: Maryland men’s basketball vs. Oregon preview
summary: The Terps come up against a conference foe desperate to earn a win at the Players Era Tournament.
content: The University of Men’s Basketball Team was defeated by the University of Virginia 87-83 on November 13th, 2026 at the Xfinity Center. | Jessie Reider/Testudo Times Through two Players Era Tournament games, Maryland men’s basketball has had two losses by a combined 12 points. The Terps’ two Players Era losses last year came by a combined 72 points. While the games have been closer, the manner of defeat has arguably been more frustrating for Terps fans. With 5:31 remaining in its game against San Diego State, the Terps led, 63-57. Head coach Buzz Williams opted to call a timeout right after Mike McNair Jr.’s 3-pointer doubled the advantage. From that point on, the Terps went 3-of-11 and squandered a late lead for the second time in two weeks. “We have called it winning time, and we didn’t do what’s required to win,” Williams said. “I think we’ll continue to get the same lesson until we embrace the difficulty of what it takes to close the game down.” The Terps will get the opportunity to put together something better in winning time when they face the Oregon Ducks in the seventh-place game of the Michelob Ultra Arena bracket, a conference matchup that has come early. The game will tip off at 3:30 p.m. ET and be available to watch on ESPNU. Oregon Ducks (3-3, 0-0 Big Ten) 2025-26 record: 12-20, 5-15 Big Ten Following the sudden retirement of longtime coach Dana Altman in October, Tony Stubblefield was named interim head coach for the Ducks. He was an assistant under Altman from 2010-2021 and 2024-2026, spending the three years in between as the head coach at DePaul and going 28-54 — including getting just nine wins in the conference. The experienced Ducks squad has started slowly under Stubblefield. Preseason action included losses against Seattle University and Utah, two schools not renowned for their recent basketball achievements, and a win over Stanford. Three mid-major wins followed, but Oregon is on a three-game losing streak, having dropped games to Oregon State, No. 13 St. John’s and No. 5 Texas Tech. The game against the Red Raiders was close, though — the Ducks held their opponents to three points over an eight-minute stretch in the second half to take the lead, but Oregon itself scored just one point over the final four minutes to hand the game back. Players to watch Malique Ewin, senior center, 6-foot-10, No. 12 — Ewin has been an all-action option for Oregon from the center spot. After stops at Ole Miss, Florida State and Arkansas, he has found a new gear in his final season of eligibility. Ewin averages 9.7 points and 9.8 rebounds per game while also chipping in just under four assists a night. Jasper Johnson, sophomore guard, 6-foot-5, No. 2 — Johnson came to Oregon after having a limited role at Kentucky his freshman year. He has earned more runs as the season has progressed, averaging 16.5 points per game over the Ducks’ last four outings to prove his worth in the midrange. Andrew Meadow, senior forward, 6-foot-7, No. 8 — Meadow has been a reliable presence over the last three seasons, starting 72 of 74 games while shooting 46% or better from the floor every year. The Boise State transfer — who got his 15 minutes of fame for his senior year makeover — had perhaps his best game as a Duck against Texas Tech, scoring 15 points and adding two rebounds against the elite Red Raiders. Strength Shooting efficiency. Oregon shoots 37.3% from 3-point range, 61st-best in the country, but it’s on 2-pointers that the Ducks shine as a team. They’re 141-of-229 on shots inside the arc, with their effective field goal percentage of 59.6% top-20 nationally. Weakness Free throws. The Ducks have struggled to get to the line this season, shooting just 103 free throws through six games, the fewest in the Big Ten. When they have gotten there, it hasn’t been very fruitful — Oregon has made just under 69% of their attempts, which ranks outside the top 200 of the NCAA. Three things to watch 1. Time advantage to the Terps. Maryland’s opponents tipped off their Thanksgiving Day game at 11:30 p.m. ET, over 10 hours after when the Terps began their game. The Ducks will have just about 14 hours of rest coming into the game, which should give Maryland a fitness edge. 2. The bench is getting shorter. The Terps again utilized 10 players against San Diego State, but Austin Brown and Robert Jennings II each played just five minutes, with all of that action coming in the first half. The pair also combined for just eight minutes in the Tennessee game. 3. Can Pharrel Payne get back on track? The Terps’ star player has struggled over the last two games, going a combined 2-for-10 from the floor while also only pulling in nine total rebounds across 41 minutes. The frontcourt issues have extended beyond just him, but his return to form will be critical for Maryland. “I don’t think [Payne] has played well in either game in Vegas,” Williams said. “What I would say categorically, not just specific to [Payne] … our decisions at the rim were really poor.”

title: Meadow scores 28, Payne 23 and Oregon defeats Maryland for 7th place at Players Era 16
summary: (AP) — Andrew Meadow scored a career-high 28 points, Fred Payne had 23, and Oregon rolled past Maryland 88-73 on Friday in the seventh-place game at the Players Era 16.Meadow, a transfer from Boise State, and Payne, who transferred from Boston College, combined to make 22 of 30 shots while the Ducks hit 57% as a team.
content: LAS VEGAS, Nev. (AP) — Andrew Meadow scored a career-high 28 points, Fred Payne had 23, and Oregon rolled past Maryland 88-73 on Friday in the seventh-place game at the Players Era 16. Meadow, a transfer from Boise State, and Payne, who transferred from Boston College, combined to make 22 of 30 shots while the Ducks hit 57% as a team. The Ducks had only six turnovers compared to Maryland's 15. Oregon had a 21-7 advantage in turning turnovers into points. Mike McNair Jr. and Pharrel Payne each scored 15 points, Baba Oladotun 12 off the bench, and Kaden House 11 for Maryland (3-5). Jasper Johnson scored 10 for Oregon (4-3). Maryland managed one field goal in the first 7 1/2 minutes of the second half and Oregon's 15-0 run contributed to a 58-40 lead. The Terrapins made only six field goals through the first 17 minutes of the half while Oregon maintained a big lead — a dunk by Meadow giving the Ducks an 84-61 lead. Meadow scored 10 points in a 12-0 run that gave the Ducks an 18-10 lead eight minutes into the game. The Ducks' lead was 30-29 before Meadow hit a 3-pointer and Seven Spurlock followed with a dunk to restore a five-point cushion. Meadow had 15 points in the half and Oregon led 40-35 at the break. title: No. 14 Vanderbilt Basketball Continues Unbeaten Start With Another Dominant Win
summary: Commodores Set the Tone Early No. 14 Vanderbilt continued its impressive start to the 2026-27 season Friday afternoon, delivering a dominant 111-56 victory over Southern at Memorial Gymnasium. The Commodores entered the matchup looking to protect their undefeated record and build momentum heading into a challenging stretch of their schedule. They accomplished both goals, controlling the game from the opening minutes and showing why they…
content: Photo by: Steve Roberts Commodores Set the Tone Early No. 14 Vanderbilt continued its impressive start to the 2026-27 season Friday afternoon, delivering a dominant 111-56 victory over Southern at Memorial Gymnasium. The Commodores entered the matchup looking to protect their undefeated record and build momentum heading into a challenging stretch of their schedule. They accomplished both goals, controlling the game from the opening minutes and showing why they are becoming one of the teams to watch in college basketball. Vanderbilt wasted little time establishing its advantage. The Commodores jumped out to a 25-8 lead, using efficient shooting and aggressive defense to put Southern in an early hole. The Jaguars struggled to find consistent offense, while Vanderbilt continued to get quality looks from both inside and outside the three-point line. The Commodores’ shooting was especially impressive during the first half. Vanderbilt connected on seven of its first 11 three point attempts and shot better than 60% from the field before halftime. Vanderbilt’s Offense Finds Its Rhythm One of the biggest positives from Friday’s performance was Vanderbilt’s ability to knock down outside shots. After experiencing some shooting struggles in recent games, the Commodores appeared much more comfortable from beyond the arc. Ace Glass III was one of the biggest contributors, finishing with 18 points. Bangot Dak also scored 18 points, giving Vanderbilt another important scoring option. Tyler Tanner and Berke Buyuktuncel added 14 points apiece, helping make the Commodores’ offense difficult to defend. Rather than relying on one player to carry the scoring load, Vanderbilt received contributions throughout its rotation. The Commodores also received an impressive performance from freshman Anthony Brown Jr. He finished with 11 points, a career high 10 assists and five rebounds. His ability to create opportunities for teammates was another encouraging development for Vanderbilt. Vanderbilt carried a comfortable 51-28 advantage into halftime, leaving Southern with a difficult challenge in the second half. Defensive Pressure Leads to a Blowout The Commodores showed no interest in allowing Southern to make the game competitive after halftime. Vanderbilt opened the second half with an 11-2 run before eventually putting together a devastating 22-0 stretch. Southern went more than seven minutes without scoring during that run, allowing the Commodores to turn a comfortable lead into an overwhelming advantage. Vanderbilt’s defense limited Southern to just 27% shooting from the field. The Commodores also dominated the glass, winning the rebounding battle 45-30, and recorded nine blocked shots. The Jaguars struggled to find answers against Vanderbilt’s size, athleticism and defensive pressure. Southern finished with just 56 points, while Vanderbilt continued adding to its lead throughout the second half. Vanderbilt Improves to 8-0 The victory moves Vanderbilt to 8-0 on the season, continuing an undefeated start that has the Commodores gaining attention nationally. Beyond the final score, Friday’s performance offered several encouraging signs. Vanderbilt rediscovered its outside shooting, received production from multiple players and showed it could dominate defensively. The Commodores will now turn their attention toward a tougher stretch of competition, beginning with a road matchup against Notre Dame in the ACC/SEC Challenge on December 2. If Vanderbilt can carry Friday’s shooting and defensive intensity into those upcoming games, the Commodores could continue building a strong case as one of the SEC’s top teams. title: UNC vs. West Virginia Live Discussion
summary: Can the Heels send the Mountaineers home to the place they belong with a loss?
content: Nov 23, 2026; Chapel Hill, North Carolina, USA; North Carolina Tar Heels mascot Rameses during the second half against the Monmouth Hawks at Smith Center. Mandatory Credit: Zachary Taft-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The Tar Heels are in Charlotte to face off against West Virginia as part of the Dick Vitale Invitational. The Heels are going into this one with just one loss on the season, while the Mountaineers have two losses, both of which were against ranked teams. This will likely be the Heels’ toughest test so far, but this is also a bit of a different team from the one that played Georgia. Having Cameron Fens in the lineup has made a difference, and one would argue that Terrence Brown playing point guard in Neo Avdalis’ absence has had more of a positive impact on the team than a negative. The thing, though, is his ability to be a facilitator will be tested big in a big way tonight. The Mountaineers are currently averaging 8 steals per game, which is slightly higher than what Carolina has been doing. Having a team that is that active on defense when you do not have your starting point guard can be tough, so we’ll see if Brown is able to take care of the ball. On the flip side, West Virginia is also averaging 9.8 turnovers per game, which funny enough is also somewhat similar to UNC’s numbers. This game will ultimately come down to who can take care of the ball better and who will be able to rebound, but of course neither matter if the ball isn’t going into the basket. Given how aggressive the Heels have been in the paint — mostly because of the crazy stuff Brown has been able to do — it’s hard to see scoring being the big issue tonight. For anybody that didn’t make the trip to Charlotte, feel free to hang out with us in the comments section. As always, we will be back later with post-game analysis and takes. Until then, Go Heels!

title: Wes Enis' 20 points help Creighton beat TCU 95-87
summary: LAS VEGAS (AP) — Wes Enis scored 20 points, including five during a decisive late-game stretch, and Creighton beat TCU 95-87 on Thursday in the Players Era 16.The Bluejays (6-1) advance to Friday’s bracket championship against the winner of Baylor and No.
content: LAS VEGAS (AP) — Wes Enis scored 20 points, including five during a decisive late-game stretch, and Creighton beat TCU 95-87 on Thursday in the Players Era 16. The Bluejays (6-1) advance to Friday’s bracket championship against the winner of Baylor and No. 22 Gonzaga after scoring at least 90 points in two straight games for the first time since November 2024. TCU (5-2) erased a nine-point halftime deficit and led 81-80 with 3:43 remaining. Enis answered with a 3-pointer 26 seconds later and added a jumper with 2:32 left to give Creighton an 85-83 lead it never surrendered. Brock Harding converted a three-point play to pull TCU within 87-86 with 1:43 remaining, but Jasen Green blocked Harding’s layup on the Horned Frogs’ next possession. Green made two free throws, and Hudson Greer scored with 42 seconds left to push the lead to 91-87. BJ Davis added 17 points for Creighton, while Greer scored 13 off the bench. Jackson McAndrew and Austin Swartz each had 11. Harding finished with 19 points, 10 assists, seven rebounds and four steals for TCU. DJ Thomas scored 17 off the bench, and Micah Robinson added 13 points and seven assists. Creighton shot 55% from the field. Up next TCU: At Notre Dame on Dec. 5. title: Why Rick Barnes says Braeden Lue is on 'monster' run for Tennessee in Las Vegas
summary: Rick Barnes said senior forward Braeden Lue has been "a monster" for Tennessee basketball as it continues rolling defensively with a win vs. Iowa State.
content: LAS VEGAS − In its two wins at the Players Era Festival, Tennessee basketball has held top scorers Pharrel Payne, who entered the tournament averaging 19.6 points per game for Maryland , to five points, and Trey Singleton, averaging 18.6 points for Iowa State, to eight. And after the Vols dispatched the Cyclones with more suffocating defense at Michelob ULTRA Arena on Nov. 26, sophomore forward DeWayne Brown II said there’s one reason why even those talented forwards struggled to put the ball in the basket. “We put B-Lue on ‘em,” he said. “B-Lue” is Braeden Lue, the 6-foot-8, 243-pound transfer from Kennesaw State who logged eight rebounds, three blocks, a steal and more solid individual defense that went beyond the box score as No. 11 Tennessee (7-0) won 75-64 against Iowa State (4-2) on Nov. 26. By beating Iowa State, the Vols have advanced to the third round of the Players Era Festival, where they'll meet the winner of No. 13 St. John's vs. No. 23 Louisville on Nov. 27 (9 p.m. ET, ESPN). A win over the Red Storm or Cardinals would send them to the event's championship game on Nov. 28 (10:30 p.m. ET, ESPN). Lue was an important reason why the Vols dominated defensively against the Cyclones, holding them to 30.6% shooting, the second-lowest by a Tennessee opponent this season, and 0.928 points per possession. “Tremendous,” Tennessee coach Rick Barnes said. “Lue just gives us that physicality. He competes. He's put together a run here four or five games where he's just been really a monster for us on the glass and doing the dirty work. “And he can defend. … We hope he can continue to build because we think he'll be able to guard anybody on the court eventually.” In only 19 minutes per game this season, Lue has excelled at finishing possessions with a defensive rebound, something Tennessee has struggled mightily to do consistently. And he has become a tone-setter for the strong defensive performances which have powered the Vols’ seven-game winning streak that opened this season. “He’s just a junkyard dog. He’s an everyday guy. He knows his role. He knows what he has to do to get us to the next level and he’s really answering that challenge right now,” sophomore guard Jalen Haralson said. “So he’s a guy that we can switch at the four, on smaller guards, big guys. He’s a junkyard dog.” In two preseason exhibitions and the first three games of the regular season, the Vols looked incapable of meeting the high defensive standards Barnes has set during his tenure as coach. Now, they are on a roll, playing a brand of defense that more closely resembles successful Vols teams of the past. Tennessee has allowed opponents to shoot only 26.9% from the field and score 56.5 points per game during a four-game stretch that began with the record-setting victory over Michigan State in Knoxville on Nov. 17. “I think what happened (in the exhibition) at Duke was probably the best thing that ever happened to us, because in that game, we just thought we were just going to shoot the ball and we got embarrassed,” Barnes said. “And after that, we've been on an uptick and we've got a chance to be so much better, too.” Lue’s counting stats during this stretch have been modest - two points, 4.5 rebounds and 0.75 blocks over 18 minutes per game. But his teammates and Barnes insist that Lue has been as crucial to the team’s early success on defense as anyone. Brown is far from surprised with Lue’s steady contributions, because this is what the Vols get from him all the time. “He’s basically doing what he does in practice every day,” Brown said. “He’s just translating it to the game.” Stephen Thompson covers Tennessee Volunteers men's basketball. Email him at stephen.thompson@knoxnews.com and follow him on X @stephenethom. title: Arizona Diamondbacks trade Tim Tawa to Pirates for catcher
summary: The Arizona Diamondbacks made moves for new players on Friday, Nov. 27, including a catcher and pitcher.
content: The Diamondbacks were active on the Major League Baseball player market on Friday, Nov. 27, adding a catcher and reportedly signing an effective pitcher from Japan. Arizona traded utility player Tim Tawa to the Pittsburgh Pirates in exchange for catcher Henry Davis, giving the team depth rising star Gabriel Moreno. Davis, 27, appeared in 97 games for the Pirates in 2026. Known more for his defense, Davis had a percentage of 45.9 runners caught stealing, which led all big league catchers that played 80 games or more. Davis hit .172 with 10 home runs and 38 runs batted in last season. In four seasons, the No. 1 overall pick in the 2021 draft hit .178. Tawa made his major league debut with the Diamondbacks in 2025, and last season played in 104 games with 351 at-bats. Primarily a first baseman and outfielder, Tawa hit .240 with 11 home runs and 42 runs batted in for the 2026 season. The Diamondbacks are reportedly in agreement with Japanese right-handed starting pitcher Kona Takahashi, who went 9-6 for the Seibu Lions in Japan last season with a 2.54 earned run average. Takahashi, who will be 30 years old when the season starts, had 114 strikeouts and 47 walks in 138 ⅓ innings in 2026. That deal is being reported by several outlets. title: Black Friday Deals: 5 Bargain Free Agents Who Could Make Sense for Pirates
summary: The Pittsburgh Pirates have not yet made a free agent addition this offseason. Perhaps they have been waiting for Black […]
content: The Pittsburgh Pirates have not yet made a free agent addition this offseason. Perhaps they have been waiting for Black Friday to come in hopes of looking for a bargain. Pittsburgh’s free agent priority is second baseman Brandon Lowe, who remains unsigned with just a few days before the start of an inevitable lockout. Lowe won’t come cheap, but the Pirates could be looking for better deals to fill out the rest of their roster. Free agency has been active over the last week or so, and a handful of players have signed or more than originally thought. But there are several remaining free agents who could fit the Pirates’ price range and provide a meaningful impact. Here are five potential bargains for the Pirates to consider. LHP Matthew Boyd The Pirates currently have a full rotation but could still look to add a left-handed starting pitcher. The market for southpaw starters has been rolling, and several options who looked like fits such as Kris Bubic, David Peterson and Patrick Sandoval signed lucrative deals. If the Pirates want to add a left-handed starter, maybe they can get Boyd for less than some others have already signed for. The 35-year-old is a 12-year veteran and had a nice two-year run with the Chicago Cubs from 2025-26. He was an All-Star last year and went 10-5 with a 3.91 ERA in 22 starts this year. LHP Sean Newcomb One alternative for the Pirates instead of adding a traditional starter is a bulk left-hander who could theoretically make spot starts if needed. After bouncing between the minors and majors from 2020-24, Newcomb has hit his stride the last two years. The 33-year-old made 60 appearances/six starts for the Chicago White Sox this year, totaling 90.1 innings. He went 2-5 with a 3.09 ERA and four saves. INF Edmundo Sosa The Pirates need a player capable of handling left-handed pitching. They also have a need in the infield. Sosa, an eight-year veteran who has split his career between the Philadelphia Phillies and St. Louis Cardinals, checks both boxes. The 30-year-old had a down 2026 season but has been essentially a league-average bat for his career. He also owns a career .273 batting average and an .806 batting average against left-handed pitching. Sosa has played shortstop, second and third base in his career and played 32 games in left field this year. LHP José Alvarado Sticking with former Phillies, Alvarado could be on the Pirates’ radar with a glaring need for a left-handed reliever. Alvarado, 31, struggled this year, finishing 5-6 with a 5.86 ERA in 68 appearances. He did, however, have a 3.82 FIP with 70 strikeouts in 58.1 innings. Alvarado was suspended for PED use last year but has been effective for much of his career. There’s some risk, but he should be affordable coming off a disappointing season. LHP Brock Burke Burke quietly had an excellent season with the Cincinnati Reds this year. The 30-year-old led the National League with 77 appearances and went 6-5 with a 2.30 ERA and a pair of saves. He struck out 74 batters in 74.1 innings. Since the start of the 2025 season, only three MLB relievers have made more appearances than Burke (145). During that time, he’s gone 13-6 with a 2.78 ERA.
