title: Chicago Cubs Make History After Latest Free Agency Signings
summary: By shattering records with five $100 million contracts in a single year, the North Siders have transformed from frugal spenders into aggressive titans of the open market.
content: The Chicago Cubs have not shied away from spending money over the past year. For many offseasons in a row, Cubs fans were often displeased with the team’s spending habits. For one of the richest teams in baseball, it was disappointing how reluctant the front office was to spend on elite players. However, the Cubs have changed their ways a bit. They have definitely been willing to spend more on high-level players in recent years. Since March of 2026, the front office has given out five $100+ million contracts. Chicago first signed Alex Bregman to a massive five-year, $175 million contract last offseason. That was the third-biggest contract that the organization has ever given out in its history. Jason Heyward’s eight-year, $184 million deal and Dansby Swanson’s seven-year, $177 million deal came in at just a bit higher. The Cubs signed Pete Crow-Armstrong to a six-year, $115 million contract in March of 2026. That contract is looking like an absolute steal, especially after Crow-Armstrong had an MVP season in 2026. The front office then extended Nico Hoerner to a six-year, $141 million deal in late March of 2026. The deal was done a few days into the regular season and locks Hoerner in Chicago through the 2032 season. This offseason, the Cubs kept spending their money to improve their roster. The front office gave Trevor Rogers a five-year, $120 million contract and gave Teruaki Sato a six-year, $120 million deal shortly after. Chicago needed some pitching help and acquired one of the top remaining left-handed starters on the open market. Rogers has a 3.16 ERA and 260 strikeouts since the start of the 2025 season. The southpaw will be that frontline starter. The Cubs also needed some power in their lineup after losing Seiya Suzuki and Ian Happ to free agency. Well, the team got that by acquiring one of the top power hitters on the open market. Sato has hit 79 home runs with 208 RBI over the past two seasons in teh Nippon Professional Baseball Organization. Giving out those five $100 million contracts since March actually puts the Cubs in the history books. They became the first team in MLB history to sign five players to over $100 million contracts in a single calendar year (according to ESPN Insights). While the Cubs have been hesitant to splurge on elite players like Shohei Ohtani, Juan Soto, and Tarik Skubal in recent offseasons, the front office deserves some credit for how it has spent money recently.

title: Dodgers Sign Utility Man Eric Wagaman To Minor League Deal
summary: The Dodgers added depth with Eric Wagaman. See his stats, the contract details, and what this means for the roster in this quick breakdown.
content: Credit: Ron Chenoy-Imagn Images The Los Angeles Dodgers made their first move of the free agency period by signing veteran utility man Eric Wagaman. According to Francys Romero of Beisbol FR, the agreement constitutes a minor league contract including a spring training invitation. This comes as the team has not added any big names to the roster yet. The signing happens just before an expected lockout that will pause most team operations. Wagaman brings experience from the New York Mets, Miami Marlins, and Minnesota Twins. He is 29 years old and can play first base, third base, or the corner outfield spots, according to Sports Illustrated . While he did not make the Opening Day roster last year, he has seen time in the big leagues with three different clubs. The Dodgers need depth players who can step in when starters get hurt or need rest. A Proven Track Record of Grit Wagaman has shown he can handle the pressure of major league games. He made his debut with the Los Angeles Angels in September 2024 after being selected in the Rule 5 draft. That season, he appeared in 18 games and hit two home runs with a .673 OPS. His time with the Miami Marlins was his most productive year. He played in 140 games, hit nine home runs, and drove in 53 runs. He also posted a .674 OPS that season. Even though his batting average was .250, he showed he could be a reliable bat off the bench or in a starting role. His journey was not a straight line to success. He started with the New York Yankees in 2017 but never reached the big leagues there. He moved to the Angels, then the Marlins, and finally the Twins before landing with the Mets. In New York this past season, he struggled a bit, hitting .191 in 26 appearances. He was designated for assignment and then elected free agency. This move shows he is willing to fight for a spot again. He knows what it takes to stay in the game. Smart Roster Depth for the Future The minor league deal is a low-risk move for the Dodgers. Since he is not on the 40-man roster, he can still talk with the team during the lockout. This gives him a head start when camp opens. He will have a chance to impress the coaches and earn a spot on the big league team. Santiago Espinal’s 2026 actions mirror this situation. Wagaman will likely start the year at Triple-A Oklahoma City. If the team needs a fill-in at first base or third base, he will be ready to go. The Marlins have been quiet in free agency while other teams sign big names until Wednesday, signing a $6.5 one-year contract with veteran catcher Gary Sanchez

title: Should fans measure the St. Louis Cardinals by wins (and losses)?
summary: 2022 seems so long ago
content: The end-of-season 2022 standings … the last time W-L meant much | From MLB.com A fun and thought-provoking conversation between Derrick Goold the Post-Dispatch and our own VEB writers here sparked an idea for an article, one that seems well timed for a post-Thanksgiving, pre-lockout respite. In that podcast, a discussion broke out centered around the question of when can Cardinal fans begin to measure the team on number of wins (and losses) again. Goold pointed out the fascinating dichotomy that the Cardinals were, by wins and losses, actually a worse team in 2026 (77 wins) than they were in 2025 (78 wins), yet fans seem to generally think it was a better season. What?!?! Those were the words that came out. The face perhaps read slightly differently, as in “What the [heck]?!?!” Derrick’s own summary (from X-Twitter) read thusly: This was a good discussion about how every fan can, maybe even should, measure the #stlcards by wins period — and how when the team isn’t doing that it creates a disconnect. Some of you may recall an article I wrote entitled “ Cardinals have an attendance problem ”. The closing line of that article resonated with a fair number of readers (also fans). The whole article struck a chord as the readership has outrun that of any other article I’ve written by like 10,000 viewers. The closing line? It makes one wonder how much of the “connection” the team has with its fanbase has been disrupted. And how they get that back. Or IF get they get that back. I’ve had in the back of my mind to come back to this topic. The podcast provided the impetus. Do those two ideas tie together? The idea of a team not measuring itself on Wins-Losses and the idea of a team has had its rather unique fan relationship disrupted? It got me to thinking about how I (perhaps “we”) measure the Cardinals, and the product they put on the field. Is it really about wins? Or World Championships? Or playoff appearances? To dig a little deeper: Why am I a fan? Why do I spend money? Why do I follow the team? How do I measure them? Am I different or is my experience typical of a larger fan cohort? Some thoughts fell out, as follows: First off, I’m a fan of the game of baseball. I watch baseball at all levels and spend time helping young children learn to play. I drag my wife, kids and grandkids to games all along the west coast, including right here at home where the SF Giants High-A team plays and the Savanah Banana’s make an odd appearance. Aside from the hoot provided by little kids running the wrong way on the bases, my first two impressions of a team or even just a game are 1) was the atmosphere relaxed and comfortable? And 2), was the game well played? Nothing will ruin an outing faster than drunken Bubba screaming profanities at the umpire from section 321 or otherwise making everyone around him uncomfortable, while the ushers make themselves scarce. Or that over-bearing parent who screams at little Caden for missing a ground ball (the first of his life!). Talk about a wet blanket. Likewise, a big-league game that is poorly executed is something that turns me off, led by pitchers who can’t throw strikes. I like good (great) pitching. I also like offense, but I can’t stand interminable at-bats of pick-and-nibble by the man on the mound. Game in, game out, these features will influence my long-term perspective on the team more than a win or a loss. My favorite time of the season is Spring Training. It isn’t the best baseball sometimes, as the latter part of games devolve into AA scrimmages, but the atmosphere is undefeated. Warm (gratefully, after a long winter) and relaxed. Even the John Deere Lawn Mower Guy is akin to a requiem for winters’ harsh grip. Wandering around timelessly to watch bonus baseball on the back fields doesn’t hurt, either. The ubiquitous sounds of ball to leather or ball to bat touches the soul. If one wanted to measure my fandom, I spend more money going to Spring Training baseball than I do any other baseball event. Clearly, then, I must not measure the Cardinals by wins and losses, because I don’t even pay attention to W-L in spring and could care less about the Grapefruit League Championship. However, I follow the Cardinals, not just any baseball team. Why? Let’s be real. Brand loyalty is a thing, an innate thing that affects me, too. I started out, long ago as a Cardinal fan because I got free tickets as a kid from the P-D/Cardinals Straight A tickets program. I couldn’t tell you who won or lost those games, but I can remember watching a young Gary Carter hit one of his first career HR off an aging Bob Gibson. So maybe I’ve never measured in W-L. Not then, not now. There are three main parts to brand loyalty (the hook, delighting the customer, and retention). Baseball, like any product, has to delight a customer in some way and be priced in a way that they perceive as a good value. If not, they won’t come back and buy again. Brand loyalty brings customers back. Baseball has an interesting loyalty generation scheme. Something has to hook us, just like another other product, but after it does, we can follow and consume that product for virtually nothing (even though we still spend). Very clever! I can follow the Cardinal’s radio broadcasts ~180 times a year for the mere pittance of $5/month MLB AtBat/Gameday Audio subscription. Something on the order of 30 CENTS per game. Now there is stretching your entertainment dollar! With AirBuds and my own John Deere Lawn Mower, I can do chores and consume the game all at once. And I can read VEB for free! And later, when I get a little extra time in life and money in my pocket, I drag Mrs. ORSTLCardsfan and grandkids to various venues and buy tickets (and food). Once hooked, the team has to provide the return customer an experience that doesn’t fail in the atmosphere and quality expectations all too often (everyone has a bad day now and again, especially if Bubba is in the house) and must occasionally exceed those expectations, sometimes wildly, repeating the delight we originally experienced eons ago. As for delight, I can remember the euphoria at the end Game 7 of the 1982 World Series more than I can remember the game itself. Delighting your customers is never a bad thing, if you want to build brand loyalty. 12 World Championships means they’ve thrilled us to the max more than once, which is even better. Playing in a World Series is no bad consolation. I’ve watched 1968, 1982, 1985, 1987, 2004, 2006, 2011 and 2013. Long time spans, but memories of unbridled joy span years, if not decades (just ask a Cubs fan). Much in the same way the smells of Grandma’s kitchen linger in our mind a generation later. In between those highlight moments, I’ve wondered if the greatness I experience game-in, game-out that brings me back is really the broadcasters I listened to, first on my transistor radio and now on my iPhone (which bears an eerie resemblance). Haray Caray->Jack Buck->Mike Shannon->John Rooney is an endless line of easy listening and consummate storytelling that has made me wonder if the stars the Cardinals really rely on are in the booth. When I read all the moaning and complaining about broadcasters on the VEB boards, I become convinced. While the best announcer can’t make a bad team good, the Cubs were rarely while Haray Carey was, and they have a loyal fan base. That brand loyalty certainly wasn’t built on Championships, or even a positive W-L record. Once brand loyalty is established, a company has to keep it. It seems to me that the string of World Series appearances (or otherwise successful seasons), the daily radio broadcasts, the price point for being a fan and the overall atmosphere of the game has more to do with my loyalty than the number of W-L in a given season. Obviously, the wins and losses has to be good in order to make the World Series, but it doesn’t have to be good every year or every home stand. But does loyalty have an expiration date? Do wins and losses even play a part in my fandom, or brand loyalty? I suppose. Where I feel it is when I look at the game I’m going to – the teams, the pitching matchup, etc. and I find myself expecting the team to win. Looking forward to an event is better than dreading it. Even when they don’t actually win, it is nicer to expect them to and be surprised when they don’t. Moreso than expecting them to be bad and being surprised when they aren’t. I mean, it never hurts for a business to pleasantly surprise, but not a great strategy to under-perform consistently and then surprise when they actually do well. The Cardinals, unfortunately, now tread in these waters. Probably the last element touches back on the atmosphere of the game and how it hooks us. Baseball is a family event for many, one that spans (and binds) generations. My dad saw Red Schoendienst as one of the best second basemen in the NL. I knew him as a kindly old man on a golf cart in spring. I saw Willie McGee and Ozzie Smith in their (phenomenal) athletic prime. My grandson sees Willie and Ozzie as greybeards in spring but admired the hip-hop that is Tai Peete. I, perhaps more than he, recognize the lineage and linkage that binds. As to how the atmosphere that permeates baseball and captures us fans and builds brand loyalty like no other … I can call my grandson in Denver and ask him if he wants to go to a baseball game and the answer will be YES with a huge smile. Good food (for those who consider ballpark dogs and cotton candy good, which kids often do). He doesn’t care (or know) that the Rockies lost 100 games. He is thrilled to go. Turns out, delighting a customer’s grandchild is a good strategy, too. This summer, he played on his first team and I brought to him one of my old leather, weather worn infielder gloves to replace the cheap, plastic glove mom and dad got him (they don’t understand ball). I think he sleeps with that glove. He has a connection to baseball, but not yet a brand loyalty to the Cardinals. That may come with time, or it may not. I deeply suspect that if the Rockies become good and make the playoffs and I take him to a game, he would be delighted and they will win his heart. And it won’t really matter a wit if they win, or lose.

title: Free agent urgency increases with lockout looming
summary: News to know about your San Diego Padres and MLB for November 27, 2026.
content: SAN DIEGO, CALIFORNIA - OCTOBER 05: General manager A. J. Preller of the San Diego Padres looks on during NLDS Workouts at Petco Park on October 05, 2026 in San Diego, California. (Photo by Orlando Ramirez/Getty Images) | Getty Images It is now or never for the San Diego Padres — well, maybe not never, but the Padres have to address their roster with Dec. 1 just days away which could result in a lockout. San Diego has been rumored to be “in” on multiple players but those rumors have proven to be just that to this point in the offseason. The problem is the Padres are getting a reputation for being linked to players who often end up signing elsewhere, which leads some to believe that players and agents are using the franchise to boost their contract lengths and values in other markets. Padres general manager A.J. Preller has the reputation of being an unpredictable and creative architect, which is what makes many of the rumors about players being linked to San Diego seem so plausible. The difference this offseason compared to others is new owners Jose E. Feliciano and Kwanza Jones. They made a bold proclamation when they were introduced to the Padres’ fanbase stating they were “all-in” and willing to do whatever was needed to bring a World Series championship to San Diego. The meaning of the phrase “all-in” was called into question earlier this offseason and that coupled with the news Feliciano and Jones were buying the Los Angeles Sparks of the WNBA for $750 million and the lack of free agent signings to this point understandably has fans on guard. The latest rumors have the Padres working to make a deal with starter Michael King, adding a bat in free agent outfielder Seiya Suzuki and potential trade packages involving one of Freddy Fermin or Luis Campusano. Will any of it come to fruition? For the sack of the fanbase and their confidence in the new owners it needs to. San Diego has plenty of needs at this point in the offseason and they have watched as National League contenders like the New York Mets and Chicago Cubs have made additions to get better and even NL West foe the Colorado Rockies have been active this offseason. Preller and the Padres need something more than Ryan Weiss, JoJo Romero, an extension of Gavin Sheets and some minor league additions if they want to avoid the backlash from failing to come through on the stated goals of the front office. title: Henry Davis Trade Details: Pirates Send C to Diamondbacks, Land INF Tim Tawa
summary: Pittsburgh made a trade on Black Friday, sending away a catcher once considered part of the team's future.
content: Henry Davis Trade Details: Pirates Send C to Diamondbacks, Land INF Tim Tawa originally appeared on SportsNet Pittsburgh . Add SportsNet Pittsburgh as a Preferred Source by clicking here . MLB’s “Hot Stove” is heating up, and the Pirates decided to get in on the action on Black Friday. Pittsburgh traded former top pick Henry Davis to the Diamondbacks for infielder Tim Tawa. It’s the end of an era for the Pirates, as Davis was considered the franchise's future and Paul Skenes’ primary backstop. Here's what to know about Friday's Pirates trade, including the background of Pittsburgh's return. Henry Davis Trade Details Pirates received: INF Tim Tawa Diamondbacks received: C Henry Davis It's a straight one-for-one swap between the teams, as announced by the Pirates on Friday. Davis was the No. 1 pick in the 2021 MLB Draft. He went to the University of Louisville, where he earned All-American and All-Atlantic Coast Conference First-Team honors. In five minor league seasons between Greensboro, Altoona, and Indianapolis, he slashed .290/.407/.529 with 38 home runs in 189 games. Davis battled through injuries in the minors and the majors. He made his official Pirates debut in 2023. Davis was promoted to starter and became the primary catcher for Paul Skenes. One of the better defensive catchers in baseball, the 27-year-old had a 45.9% caught steeling percent mark last year. In 283 major league games, Davis has slashed .178/.295/.300 with 25 home runs. A former high school quarterback, Tawa played baseball at Stanford. He was selected in the 11th round of the 2021 MLB Draft by the Diamondbacks. Tawa was promoted to the majors in 2025. Tawa slashed .240/.297/.393 with 11 homers and 42 RBIs in 104 games last year. The Pirates will now look to replace Henry as team catcher. title: Jazz Chisholm Jr. leaving Yankees, but staying in the AL East
summary: The Jazz Chisholm Jr. saga is officially over in the Bronx, but he's got the potential to be a frequent Yankees' opponent in the AL East.
content: The Jazz Chisholm Jr. saga is officially over in the Bronx, but he's got the potential to be a frequent Yankees' opponent in the American League East. On Nov. 27, the talented but enigmatic free agent lefty-hitting second baseman agreed to a contract with the Toronto Blue Jays , per MLB.com, that could be worth up to $58.5 million through 2028. Chisholm, who turns 29 in February, is guaranteed $20 million in 2027 through a $6 million signing bonus, $12.5 million salary and a $1.5 million opt out for 2028. If Chisholm triggers the opt out, the Blue Jays are able to counter with a $40 million club option for 2028. Chisholm arrived in pinstripes at the 2024 trade deadline from Miami, went to the World Series with the Yanks (as a third baseman) and became a 30-30 (homers, steals) player in 2025, despite missing time due to injury. But in a frustrating free agent walk year in 2026, Chisholm batted .231 with a .711 OPS, 19 homers and 55 RBI in 137 games, but with 41 stolen bases this season. "I don't feel like I had a great year,'' Chisholm said after the Yankees were swept in the AL Division Series by the eventual AL champion Rays. Chisholm pledged that he wanted to remain a Yankee, having grown up as a fan, watching Derek Jeter and those championship clubs of the late '90s and 2000. "I had a great time being a Yankee,'' said Chisholm, but the club was clearly pivoting in a direction without him in 2027, with Anthony Volpe and Jose Caballero as in-house second base candidates and an eye on the trade and free agent markets. title: Marlins Need Imanaga After Sánchez Deal, Not Just Any Veteran
summary: The Marlins signed Gary Sánchez to a one-year, $6.5 million deal. Now the front office must target Shota Imanaga to fix a rotation that lacks depth.
content: Credit: Patrick Gorski-Imagn Images The Miami Marlins finally made a move this offseason by agreeing to terms with catcher Gary Sánchez on a one-year contract. A person with knowledge of the talks told The Associated Press the deal could be worth up to $6.5 million. No position player has ever received a larger contract from Peter Bendix, the president of baseball operations, in his tenure. Sánchez, who turns 34 next week, spent last season with the World Series champion Milwaukee Brewers. He hit just .209 for the title-winning club but posted a much better .801 OPS against left-handed pitching. The Marlins struggled mightily against southpaws last year, ranking 27th in wRC+ and posting an 85 wRC+ in that category. Sánchez brings a right-handed bat to a lineup that desperately needs to hit lefties better in 2027. Signing Sánchez fixes a specific hole, but it leaves the rotation wide open for a major upgrade. The front office cannot stop there if they want to build on an 80-win season. Sandy Alcantara remains the ace, and Eury Pérez showed flashes of brilliance despite an up-and-down year. Max Meyer is expected to be ready for spring training after a neck injury cut his season short. Beyond those three, the depth is thin. Janson Junk and Ryan Gusto proved serviceable, while Tyler Phillips struggled with home runs after joining the rotation. The team needs a left-handed starter who can eat innings and keep runners off base. Robbie Ray or Matthew Boyd could work as one-year stopgaps, but they are not the long-term answer. Why Imanaga Is The Missing Piece Shota Imanaga is the name the Marlins should chase to complement their young core. He has posted season ERAs of 2.91, 3.73, and 3.77 in his three seasons stateside. His ability to limit traffic on the bases is elite, with a 1.038 WHIP that ranks sixth-lowest among 36 pitchers with at least 80 starts since 2024. Fish On First reported that Imanaga has been a quality starter despite concerns about his tendency to give up the long ball. Preventing walks becomes his greatest strength when he keeps the ball in the park, with walk rates ranking in the 97th, 96th, and 95th percentiles. Preventing walks is exactly what a young rotation needs to stay out of trouble early in games. The Defense Factor And Roster Math While Sánchez offers offensive help, his defense remains a liability. He graded out as a below-average defensive catcher, recording negative six blocks above average and negative two framing. This is why the team added three catchers to the 40-man roster, including Joe Mack and Agustín Ramirez. Sánchez will likely DH or serve as a late-game pinch-hitter against left-handed pitchers. The Marlins might utilize him at first base to enhance their defense, where he has recorded a minus-one DRS. The signing gives the team a veteran presence in a young clubhouse, but it does not solve the starting pitching gap. To become legit contenders, the Marlins must immediately focus on addressing their rotation. Jeff Passan of ESPN reported the agreement on Wednesday night, setting the stage for the next big move.

title: Marlins Outfielder is Generating Trade Interest
summary: Teams around Major League Baseball may want to make serious offers for Miami outfielder Kyle Stowers
content: The Miami Marlins may have another difficult offseason decision on their hands, and this time it involves one of the most productive players in their lineup. Outfielder Kyle Stowers is reportedly generating interest from several clubs, sending rumors swirling that the team may trade him this winter. For a franchise continuing to build toward sustained contention, Stowers represents an interesting asset. He has demonstrated the ability to provide legitimate power in the middle of a lineup, but his growing value could also make him an attractive trade chip as the Marlins evaluate their roster and long-term organizational priorities. The interest is hardly surprising, and president of baseball operations Peter Bendix has taken notice. Stowers enjoyed a breakout 2025 campaign, batting .288 with 25 home runs and 73 RBI in 117 games. However, his 2026 season wasn't quite as impressive, but it shouldn't be overlooked. The youngster hit .239 with 21 home runs and 65 RBI while posting a .789 OPS, which were still solid numbers. Unfortunately, injuries have become a significant part of the conversation surrounding Stowers. He missed the first 21 games of the 2026 season with a hamstring injury, then another hamstring issue and an abdominal strain that limited him to 121 games. There is also the financial component to consider. Stowers is entering his first season of arbitration eligibility, with his 2027 salary projected to be around $3.2 million. He remains under team control through 2029, giving an acquiring club multiple seasons of relatively affordable production. Why Would Miami Trade Him? The Marlins have made it clear that their intention is to become competitive in 2027. After finishing 80-82, the organization is looking to take another step forward rather than dismantle the roster. At the same time, Miami also has several areas that need attention, particularly its pitching staff. If another organization presents an attractive package featuring controllable starting pitching or high-end prospects, Peter Bendix would have to at least consider the possibility. The Marlins have also reportedly explored adding a starting-caliber player at a corner infield or outfield position. Depending on how those discussions develop, Stowers could become somewhat expendable, particularly if Miami identifies an opportunity to improve multiple areas of its roster through a trade. Stowers is only 28, has demonstrated legitimate middle-of-the-order potential, and already has experience producing at an All-Star level. Finding a replacement via free agency could be considerably more expensive, and there is no guarantee that an outside acquisition would provide an upgrade. Unless another club makes an offer that substantially exceeds what Miami believes Stowers can provide over the next several seasons, keeping him might be the smarter baseball decision. In the end, the team must decide if some of the prospects in the organization, like rising star Dillon Lewis , could replace Stowers. Then, the more experienced and (somewhat) established player could be used as a commodity for pitching or perhaps some corner infield help. In that scenario, Bendix would have to pull the trigger. So, in many ways, it may be less about Stowers' ability and potential, and more about the teams needs and the talent the depth they have in the organization. This potential trade comes down to that type of numbers game.

title: Too Early to Panic About A's Lack of Moves This Offseason
summary: The Athletics finished with one of the worst records in MLB in 2026 and are one of the few teams that are still worse than they were when the offseason began. With more ground still to make up, it's still too early to panic about 2027.
content: Since making the first trade of the offseason, the Athletics have been fairly quiet this offseason, stacking up players on minor-league deals, but not adding a ton of impact talent to the big-league roster just yet. Teams like the Colorado Rockies have been adding pitching before the expected lockout, but the A's have stayed put. The A's lack of movement so far this winter is illustrated in this table, where each team's projected WAR change since the start of free agency is ranked. Of course the New York Mets, who signed Tarik Skubal, are at the top of the heap. The A's, meanwhile, are one of just seven clubs to have not had a positive impact this offseason. Projected WAR Change Since Start of Free Agency pic.twitter.com/7mn1WaEkRo — Thomas Nestico (@TJStats) November 26, 2026 The A's rank 27th on this list with a -1.5 WAR, and while the Milwaukee Brewers and Tampa Bay Rays rank 26th and 29th, they're also starting from a much higher point, while the A's are being left further behind. Only the Angels (62-100) and Rockies (58-104) finished with worse records than the A's 64-98 mark, but the Angels rank 21st on this table, while Colorado is astonishingly 2nd. Of course, it's still early in the overall offseason, but with the lockout set to begin on December 2, this first phase of the offseason is going to wrap up shortly. Don't Panic Just Yet While the A's haven't been active, it's still too early to panic about the team's outlook for 2027. The first reason is that there are still a few days before baseball shuts down, and there will be some time before the start of the season when free agents who are still on the market can be wooed, or trades can be made before Opening Day 2027. The other and arguably bigger reason is that the A's new front office has mentioned numerous times that development is going to be a big area of emphasis for them moving forward, and we've seen some of that at work already as the club now has president of baseball operations Taylor Smith and GM Cam Castro splitting the duties that used to be held by just David Forst. They've also hired new hitting and pitching coaches, as well as directors of both hitting and pitching to make sure the A's philosophy is preached up and down the system. With a focus on limiting walks and generating more ground balls next season, the pitching staff should be improved even with the same pitchers on the staff, thanks to the new philosophy and some of the new information that will be shared with them. The A's may not have made a huge addition to the roster just yet, but getting more out of guys like Gage Jump, Jacob Lopez and Jack Perkins would be a huge boost to the club's pitching performance in 2027.

title: Why Yankees have trade interest in 2 Padres catchers

title: Yankees could be in trouble with catcher market drying up
summary: The Yankees can take a marker to their offseason whiteboards.
content: The Yankees can take a marker to their offseason whiteboards. Cross out Tyler Stephenson, who agreed to return to the Reds. Put an “X” through Gary Sánchez, who will sign with the Marlins . Already erased was Ryan Jeffers, who surprisingly accepted the Twins’ qualifying offer. Access the Yankees beat like never before Join Post Sports+ for exciting subscriber-only features, including real-time texting with Greg Joyce about the inside buzz on the Yankees. Try it free The names, while still plentiful in number, grow less intriguing by the day. After spending two seasons without a true righty-hitting option at catcher, the Yankees still are searching for Austin Wells’ complement. “If we can find a good-defending, right-handed-hitting option to level up, that’d be great,” Yankees general manager Brian Cashman said earlier this month at the GM Meetings, “but that’s also slim pickings.” The pickings are even slimmer now. The one catcher still on the free-agent market likely to command a multiyear and not-insignificant contract is Carson Kelly. It is likely that the caliber of catcher the Yankees add will depend upon their pursuits of bullpen, center field and third base help. If they land reliever Adrian Morejon, for example, they probably would reach into the bargain bin elsewhere (unless they bring in a catcher through trade). With less than a week to go before signings and trades are expected to freeze, here are some of the righty-hitting catcher options who are still available through free agency: Carson Kelly: The best still on the board, Kelly likely expects more playing time and a better contract than the Yankees are willing to give. But a veteran, well-regarded catcher with a lifetime .822 OPS against southpaws would fit well. Austin Hedges: One of the premier framers in baseball, the 34-year-old always has been defensively excellent but not much of an offensive threat. Last season, he did hit lefties well (.747 OPS). Carson Kelly watches the action during the Cubs’ loss to the Marlins on Sept. 22, 2026, at Wrigley Field in Chicago. Getty Images James McCann: A veteran and former Met who has settled nicely into a part-time/backup role in the twilight of his career, McCann’s defense has slipped, but he has hit decently — although last season, he was stronger against righty pitching. Kyle Higashioka: Another for the run-it-back Yankees? Higashioka, now 36, has seen his pop time slow, and he caught just seven of 39 attempted base stealers last season, but he remains agile behind the plate and hit lefties well last season before suffering a flexor strain in July. Elias Díaz: His defense still was solid during his age-35 season with the Royals and Rangers this past year and he posted an .820 OPS against southpaws. Do the Yankees want a slugger with nice pop but poor on-base skills? Kyle Higashioka steps up to the plate during a Yankees-Tigers game on Sept. 7, 2023, at the Stadium. Getty Images And possible trade candidates: Iván Herrera/Pedro Pagés: The Cardinals are deep at catcher, where Leo Bernal likely will start next season after a strong debut and with top prospect Rainiel Rodríguez on the way. They could afford to part with the bat-first Herrera or glove-first Pagés. Herrera mostly served as DH last season, struggling particularly behind the plate with holding opposing base runners, but he owns an .863 OPS against lefties in his five seasons. Pagés has not hit much in his three years but is a strong defender. Freddy Fermin/Luis Campusano: After top prospect Ethan Salas got his feet wet last season, the Padres have a surplus of catchers. The 31-year-old Fermin is defensively strong but owns only a .599 OPS over his past two seasons. Campusano’s all-around defense has made strides, particularly his throwing arm, and he is coming off a strong season in which he hit .265 with a .795 OPS. Agustín Ramírez: With Sánchez landing in Miami as a complement to Joe Mack, would the Marlins shop Ramírez? Maybe not; they could store the former Yankees prospect in the minors and work on his defense, which has been weak. But the 25-year-old slugger, who went from the Yankees to the Marlins in the Jazz Chisholm Jr. trade, has a strong offensive reputation and has posted a .755 OPS against lefties in his two major league seasons.

title: Dricus Du Plessis: If the Adesanya I fought shows up at UFC Riyadh, Magomedov 'done for'
summary: Dricus Du Plessis expects Israel Adesanya to rebound at UFC Fight Night 295.
content: Dricus Du Plessis expects Israel Adesanya to rebound at UFC Fight Night 295. Former champion Adesanya (24-6 MMA, 13-6 UFC) takes on rising middleweight Shara Magomedov (17-1 MMA, 6-1 UFC) in the Dec. 5 main event in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. Adesanya will look to snap a four-fight losing skid – one of the setbacks which came in a title fight against Du Plessis at UFC 305 . Although Adesanya hasn't been getting his hand raised, he has shown shades of his championship form, and that's what Du Plessis is banking on. "It's an awesome fight, and once again with Adesanya, that's what's so great in his whole career: He's not shying away from anything," Du Plessis told Fight Forecast . "He's still taking those hard fights. 'Bullet' is an up-and-coming killer. I honestly believe Adesanya, I hope for him, and I just believe he's going to be too much for Shara because Shara 'Bullet' can do great things and he can strike, but if the Adesanya that fought me gets in there, Shara 'Bullet' is done for. Adesanya, he changed teams, so he's going to have a chip on his shoulder. "He went to go and train with (Alexander Volkanovski), and we've seen what Volk has been doing. That team has been really shaping up so, big ups to Adesanya. At the end of his career, he doesn't need to fight these killers and to change the gym now at this age and at the end of his career. He doesn't have to do that. But he's such a martial artist, he wants to be the best he can be, and the fact that he does that shows me that he's still committed to winning, not just competing. I'm excited for it, and I'm going with Izzy for that one." Adesanya parted ways with his longtime gym, City Kickboxing, to train in a more concentrated environment at Unity MMA. Du Plessis was asked if the UFC still needs Adesanya. "Right now he's almost in that Anderson Silva time in his career, at the end where Anderson was losing fights, but nobody cared," Du Plessis said. "His legacy was already cemented. He's done what he's needed for the sport, and right now I don't think the UFC needs him. I think fans love him, fans love his style, and I think he loves the sport, so I don't think it's the UFC needs him anymore. "I think he loves it so much he needs it more – not that he needs it. He needs it for himself. He loves it so much that he feels empty without it. I think that's how a lot of us feel. ... I think if he gets that big, big win, I think maybe even this fight he might call it a day. But up until, let the man fight. Let him enjoy his life because it's not like he's getting manhandled, and he's fighting the best in the world." This article originally appeared on MMA Junkie: Dricus Du Plessis: If the Adesanya I fought shows up at UFC Riyadh, Magomedov 'done for'

title: Champ Kyle Larson is On a Generational Run. Could Others Catch Up?
summary: Kyle Larson is on as close to a generational run as you can get in the current era of the NASCAR Cup Series with the NextGen car but could others catch up?
content: Kyle Larson is on as close to a generational run as you can get in the current era of the NASCAR Cup Series with the NextGen car. Larson is a three-time Cup Series champion and the winner of the last two championships, becoming the first back-to-back series champion since Jimmie Johnson won five in a row from 2006 to 2010. The highlight of Larson's season was undoubtedly his Chase run. He scored three wins, six top-five finishes, eight top-10 finishes and an average finish of 7.3 in the final 10 races. He led 579 of the 3,151 laps he completed and scored 456 points, 54 points more than any other driver. Going into the final race, Larson had an average finish of 6.78. He had four consecutive top-two finishes after the Chase opener that allowed him to basically be in control in the second half and locked it up with an actually generational win at Talladega Superspeedway. Larson and crew chief Cliff Daniels proved they're their own type of animal on another level from their competitors and trying to knock on the door of Jimmie Johnson and Chad Knaus. Now, back up three months and imagine telling someone this -- like the publisher and editor here at NASCAR Roundtable. At the end of August, confidence in Hendrick Motorsports winning the championship was slim but not zero for a reason. Larson scored no wins, nine top-fives and 13 top-10s in the first 26 races. Although they showed they weren't far off in one metric, leading 659 of the 6,328 laps they completed in the regular season, they had an average finish of 17.3. They started the Chase in the No. 7 seed, one position below the effective cutoff teams declared preseason and 55 points out of the lead. Indianapolis, Chicagoland, Nashville Superspeedway and EchoPark Speedway Atlanta in the spring all represented different times where Larson missed the mark as a driver. Yet, when the Chase started, it was game on for Larson and everyone else looked relatively semi-pro in retrospect. Has everyone caught onto their game? Maybe. Drivers like Christopher Bell, Denny Hamlin, Chase Briscoe and Ryan Blaney all could've been hoisting the Cup if one or a few little things had gone differently. Larson earned the championship with performance that was not only stellar but clean. For instance, Hamlin earned 40 or more points just once in the final nine races, while Larson did it six times. Larson didn't need to start that well because a stellar run in the Chase got them there but not every season will present that. A new Ford body is coming, Chevrolet is in its second year with a new body and Toyota's body is well-seasoned to make 2027 a challenge.

title: What New Rules Will NASCAR Have in 2027?
summary: NASCAR is making several changes, especially in the Cup Series, as 2026 ends and the 2027 season draws closer.
content: CONCORD, N.C. -- NASCAR is making several changes , especially in the Cup Series, as 2026 ends and the 2027 season draws closer. NASCAR issued a bulletin to teams Friday, Nov. 20, detailing the changes. Here are the highlights, according to what NASCAR sent the media: For the NASCAR Cup Series intermediate engine package, the horsepower level will be elevated from 670 to 750 starting at Charlotte-1. The All-Star Race will feature a horsepower level of 800 hp. After that race, NASCAR and the engine builders will do a full analysis on the race quality and engine performance. If the industry feels comfortable, NASCAR may increase to 800 hp for all Cup Series short tracks and road course starting at Bristol-2. Though not part of the Rule Book bulletin, NASCAR will implement a NCS qualifying-specific setup for Daytona and Talladega qualifying with the goal of reaching 200 mph laps. Splitter stuffers will be removed at all short tracks and road courses in the Cup Series. NASCAR has removed rules for minimum damper length in the Cup Series, giving teams further setup options. Except for the Daytona 500, if Qualifying is incomplete, the current Team Owner Points standings will be used to assign starting grid positions. Superspeedway qualifying sessions will move to one round, only. Updated wet-weather oval procedures: Once the Race has started and NASCAR has declared wet weather conditions, the crew chief will determine any tire configuration changes. NASCAR added the following language to the double painted line rule to further clarify the rule: NASCAR defines beneath the double painted lines as follows: When the vehicle’s left side tires are beneath the left line of the inside double painted lines that separate the apron from the racing surface. NASCAR clarified the rules around a driver missing a race without NASCAR approval: Before The Chase, the affected driver and/or Team owner will begin The Chase with 2,000 Points. All other qualified drivers and/or Team owners will retain the reset Points totals corresponding to their respective standing position as outlined in Table 12.4.2 Driver and Team Owner Points Adjustment. During The Chase, the affected driver and/or Team owner will have their respective Points totals reset to 2,000 Points. For the NASCAR O’Reilly Auto Parts Series, the driver/owner would reset to 2,020; in the NASCAR FedEx Freight Truck Series, the reset would be 2,030. NASCAR adjusted the minimal engine seal count: Teams considered to be full-time (i.e. entered in all Events for the current Race season) must compete in a minimum of 20 Points Events with a sealed engine during the Race season. An L3 penalty option has been added to the NASCAR O’Reilly Auto Parts Series and NASCAR FedEx Freight Truck Series.

title: 5 Potential Destinations For Deni Avdija When He Inevitably Hits Free Agency In 2028
summary: Deni Avdija's contract is one of the most team-friendly in the NBA, but it's also surely going to lead to him hitting unrestricted free agency in 2028.
content: Mandatory Credit: Bill Streicher-Imagn Images The Portland Trail Blazers have exceeded expectations at the start of this 2026-27 NBA season. The Trail Blazers are sixth in the Western Conference with a 12-6 record, and it’s Deni Avdija who has led the charge. Avdija emerged as an All-Star for the Trail Blazers last season and has carried on from where he left off. The 25-year-old is averaging 24.9 points, 6.6 rebounds, 6.1 assists, 1.1 steals, and 0.4 blocks per game while shooting 51.9% from the field and 43.3% from beyond the arc. That’s terrific production from a player who is notably in the third year of a four-year, $55 million rookie scale extension. This is quite a bargain for the Trail Blazers, but it is also a double-edged sword. You see, extensions are capped at 140% of the salary in the final year of the existing deal. Avdija will only make $11.8 million in 2027-28, so there is virtually no chance he agrees to an extension in 2027. The Trail Blazers can renegotiate and extend up to his max, but that would require them to shed a lot of salary to create cap space, a route they’re unlikely to go down. So, Avdija will almost inevitably hit unrestricted free agency in 2028. You’d think the Trail Blazers could just offer him the super max to keep him, but he isn’t eligible for it no matter how well he plays from here on out. The Trail Blazers officially acquired Avdija from the Washington Wizards in July 2024, which meant he was already in his second contract when he got traded. That makes him ineligible for the supermax. This is quite a situation that the Trail Blazers find themselves in, and here we take a look at five potential options for Avdija when he becomes an unrestricted free agent. 1. Portland Trail Blazers Now, of course, the likeliest outcome is that Avdija chooses to return to the Trail Blazers, who have his bird rights. The Israeli has repeatedly spoken about how much he loves Portland, and he is now also leading a team that can make noise in the West. Back in the offseason, the Trail Blazers were called a “sinking ship” that Avdija probably should leave in free agency, but they clearly aren’t looking like one now. If they are a playoff team in 2028 as well, he wouldn’t have to look elsewhere to be in a situation where he can play winning basketball. The Trail Blazers can also offer Avdija a five-year deal with 8% yearly raises in 2028, while other teams can only put four-year deals with 5% yearly raises on the table. He will have made $75 million in salaries when this current deal expires, which is a lot of money, but more financial security wouldn’t hurt. 2. Golden State Warriors Should things go south for the Trail Blazers in 2027-28 ( Damian Lillard and Jrue Holiday are 36), Avdija could be tempted to look elsewhere. The Golden State Warriors would be one of the teams in position to pounce. As of now, the Warriors are expected to have cap space to pursue a max player in 2028. Stephen Curry ($60.1 million) and Brandin Podziemski (20.5 million) are currently their only players set to make over $10 million in 2028-29, and the former has a player option. Going to the Warriors would mean Avdija gets to lead the post-Curry era along with Podziemski and Yaxel Lendeborg . They have a lot of draft picks they could trade to further improve that roster as well. Also, if Avdija cares, he’d be in one of the biggest markets. 3. Boston Celtics Now, the Boston Celtics aren’t projected to have a lot of cap space in 2028, but they’re going to need a co-star for Jayson Tatum . They, of course, traded away Jaylen Brown to the Philadelphia 76ers this past offseason for Paul George . George has surpassed expectations so far, but he is 36 years old and has a $56.6 million player option for 2027-28. You’d imagine the Celtics would prefer he opt out and sign a multi-year deal at a lower annual rate, but we don’t know what his intentions are. Whatever George does, he is not going to be on the Celtics’ books for $50 million in 2028. With the way Derrick White is shooting , it might be in their best interests to ship him out of town in the next year or so as well. White has a $34.8 million player option for 2028-29, and if the Celtics do manage to move off him without taking on long-term salary, they could have space for Avdija. He and Tatum would ensure they remain contenders for the foreseeable future. 4. Dallas Mavericks Going to the Dallas Mavericks would see Avdija team up with another former Duke star in Cooper Flagg . The Mavericks should have plenty of cap space in 2028 as well, but this does depend a bit on what a potential Kyrie Irving extension looks like. It won’t be difficult for them to create space, though. With Flagg already looking like a superstar with averages of 24.3 points, 6.3 rebounds, 6.7 assists, 1.8 steals, and 0.8 blocks per game as a sophomore, the Mavericks would be an intriguing landing spot for free agents. He already has them ahead of schedule, as they are right behind the Trail Blazers with an 11-7 record. It’s undoubtedly a team on the rise. 5. Memphis Grizzlies Speaking of exceeding expectations, no one has done that to the extent that the Memphis Grizzlies have. The Grizzlies are fifth in the West with a 14-5 record. While 29-year-old Ty Jerome has led the charge, this is a team with a lot of young talent like Cameron Boozer , Cedric Coward, and Zach Edey . The Grizzlies are only going to get better as time passes, and they will likely have cap space to get Avdija and elevate themselves even further. The only issue here, though, is that those Grizzlies youngsters are going to be up for significant extensions in the coming years. You can only have so many players on large contracts in this second-apron era, so they might have some reservations. Memphis has never been a popular free agent landing spot either, so Avdija might have some reservations as well, making this the least likely of the five destinations.

This has to be more than just a single supporting player, which is why the belief here remains that Erik Spoelstra somehow has to get Tim Hardaway Jr. ...
content: Q: Ira, is the Heat’s success all about how Klay Thompson shoots? When he is on, they usually win and not so much when his shot is off. – Joel, Plantation. A: Which, on one hand, seems to be the case, and on the other, also has to be a concern. This has to be more than just a single supporting player, which is why the belief here remains that Erik Spoelstra somehow has to get Tim Hardaway Jr. going. Because the reality is that Klay Thompson, like any shooter, will have an off night. The reality also is that there needs to be someone else to step up. Ryan Conwell has shown that he can do it in spurts, but a contender needs a veteran in such a role. If it truly is coming down to Klay or bust, then bust has a reasonable chance of prevailing. Related Articles Submit your “Ask Ira” question here! Q: There should be a concern that Miami cannot beat good to very good teams when the opposition is close to healthy. – Rodney. A: So perhaps that made Wednesday night in Philadelphia another wake-up call, similar to the start of the season. Even with Jaylen Brown sidelined for the second half of that game, Philadelphia presented the Heat with as much opposing wing talent as they have faced in a while. Yes, this team can score, but likely not consistently as some of the top scoring teams in the East. So that puts the onus back on the defense, which is what Erik Spoelstra said should’ve been the priority from the outset. Q: Why should we care about the NBA Cup? – Stephen. A: You’ve come to the wrong place if you are seeking some type of affirmation here. By jamming up the rest of the schedule and leading to schedule uncertainty, it’s almost as if the NBA Cup is getting in the way, rather than the in-season tournament being some type of featured attraction. For example, quick, name the previous NBA Cup champions? Exactly.

title: Cade Cunningham injury update: Pistons star gets 'time to recover'
summary: Detroit Pistons point guard Cade Cunningham will miss his second straight game against the Milwaukee Bucks on Friday, Nov. 27, and maybe more.
content: Cade Cunningham will miss his second straight game against the Milwaukee Bucks on Friday, Nov. 27 – and it sounds as though he could be out a while longer. The Detroit Pistons guard has been ruled out of the game with right knee tendinopathy. Cunningham was a late scratch on Tuesday before the Pistons' road win over the Orlando Magic . During his pregame press conference, Friday coach J.B. Bickerstaff said the team won't rush him back. With a long season ahead, the plan is to rest him until the discomfort subsides. HELLO AND GOODBYE: Cade Cunningham injury dulls hope from Jalen Duren's looming return "It’s one of those things where we’re trying our best to make sure we’re protecting him," Bickerstaff said. "We know how much he wants to play and how much he wants to be out on the floor. It’s important that he gets right. We have a long season ahead of us and we don’t want it to be one of those things where it’s back-and-forth. We want to give him some time to recover." The knee has been ailing Cunningham for more than a week – he missed a road game against the New Orleans Pelicans last Wednesday on the second half of a back-to-back and was listed as probable with the same injury entering their following games at home against the Toronto Raptors on Nov. 20 and on the road against the Atlanta Hawks on Sunday. Cunningham had his worst scoring performance of the season in Atlanta, finishing with five points on 2-for-9 shooting to go with 15 assists and four rebounds in 33 minutes. "He’s battling through a lot, and I’ll leave it at that," Bickerstaff said before the game against the Magic. "He’s gonna go out and compete and give us what he’s got, but he’s fighting through a lot." The Pistons also will be without Jalen Duren (right hamstring strain) for the 16th game in a row and Duncan Robinson (left quad strain) for the sixth game in a row. Duren practiced with the Motor City Cruise on Wednesday, a significant milestone for his impending return. Contact Omari at osankofa@freepress.com . Follow him on X and/or Bluesky . title: Dylan Harper could be back in action when Spurs host Lakers on Friday
summary: The dynamic guard has missed the last four games after suffering a hip injury in a loss to Detroit on Nov. 17.
content: San Antonio Spurs guard Dylan Harper reacts to a 3-pointer by teammate Julian Champagnie, not pictured, during the fourth quarter of an NBA game against the Los Angeles Clippers on Thursday, Nov. 19, 2026, in San Antonio. The Spurs won 124-112. (Sam Owens/San Antonio Express-News) Spurs guard Dylan Harper could make his return to the court as soon as Friday night after the team listed him as questionable for its showdown with the Los Angeles Lakers at the Frost Bank Center. Harper has missed the last four games after he suffered a left hip external rotator strain late in the Spurs' 105-93 loss to Detroit on Nov. 17. The injury was expected to sideline him for two to three weeks, but the Spurs upgraded him to questionable after Wednesday night's 116-111 loss at Portland. Harper, 20, ranks as the Spurs' second-leading scorer behind Victor Wembanyama at 18.4 points per game. He's also averaging 5.4 rebounds and 4.5 assists in 15 appearances. The Spurs are 3-1 without Harper, who has been replaced in the starting lineup by Julian Champagnie. In other injury news, the Spurs upgraded guard De'Aaron Fox to questionable after he sat out the last two games with a bruised right shin. The Spurs started Harrison Barnes the last two games to round out a starting lineup that included Stephon Castle, Devin Vassell, Champagnie and Wembanyama. Forward Tobias Harris remains out with a left calf strain. The 15-year-veteran suffered the injury early in training camp after the Spurs signed him in the offseason to a two-year, $31 million contract. Friday's NBA Cup in-season tournament group play matchup features the two top teams in the Western Conference in the Lakers (15-3) and the Spurs (15-4). title: For Heat’s Gardner, earning his keep is now a day-to-day process (until Jan. 10)

content: NEW YORK — For Myron Gardner, it again has become pay to play . . . not that the second-year Heat forward is concerning himself with such money matters. The lone Heat player at the start of the season without a fully guaranteed contract, Gardner’s $500,000 partial guarantee reached its guaranteed date on Friday. Going forward — until Jan. 10 when all NBA contracts become guaranteed for the season — he will earn an additional $12,362 per day. With the Heat working against a hard cap created by the machinations of the trade for Giannis Antetokounmpo , the flexibility with Gardner’s contract had stood as a lever to potentially upgrade the roster. But with Gardner having strung together several positive recent performances, including when filling in for three games as a starter in place of sidelined Pelle Larsson, Gardner showed that he stands as a value contract. “I’m just focused on the goal ahead, trying to win every game, get better each and every day. I ain’t really worried about the contract right now,” Gardner said, with the Heat turning their attention to Friday night’s NBA Cup game against the New York Knicks at Madison Square Gardner. While the emergence of second-round pick Ryan Conwell initially pushed Gardner further down Erik Spoelstra’s pecking order, Gardner’s energy on demand has proven valuable during stages when the Heat grow stagnant. “He amplifies groups just with his energy and his toughness,” Spoelstra said. “Yeah, he does things that sometimes agitate people, but he actually is a pretty simple basketball player. He’ll drive it when he needs to drive it. He’ll shoot it when he needs to shoot it. He’ll move it when he needs to move it. But he’s always going to be on the move. He’s always going to crash the glass. He’s always going to cut for somebody else, sacrifice. “It’s not something that we’re having to scream at him to do. It’s just what he does by his nature. And that helps all of your better players. And then defensively, he’s getting more solid and he’s fouling less.” Having the confidence of his coach, Gardner said, is what matters more than how the front office decides to work under the team’s hard cap, a situation that currently affords the Heat the ability to only add a player at the veteran minimum. “Guarantees are always going to be there, but there’s nothing I can do about that. So I’m always trying to focus on getting better. I know what I can control.” The Larsson absence and the resulting starting opportunities allayed any Gardner concerns in regard to his contract. “It was helpful, for sure, to be able to get an opportunity and try to make the most of it,” he said, with the Heat 3-0 in his starts. “It showed that every opportunity, I just got to stay ready for it.” Because with Larsson back, with Conwell playing well, and with Tim Hardaway Jr. still a veteran option, one approach could be sweating out the competition. But that’s not Gardner. Related Articles ASK IRA: Is Klay or bust a perilous path for Heat? Erik Spoelstra’s read on the Heat’s next steps? ‘It takes what it takes’ ASK IRA: Is Nikola Jovic being too easily forgotten by Spoelstra, Heat? Winderman’s view: LeBron in 76ers win reminds Heat of reunion lost Giannis returns, but Heat fall to 76ers’ Maxey, LeBron in NBA Cup game “It’s the next man up,” he said. “We emphasize competitive will over here, so that’s our culture. Everybody ready to play.” And also ready if they don’t play, while appreciating his place and his role. “I’m just making sure I’m just doing the easy part, for real, making the right play, the simple play,” he said. “I ain’t got to do nothing too crazy., just whatever the team needs.” One of the factors that has kept Keshad Johnson around the past three years has been his optimistic outlook and infectious personality. With Gardner, it is much the same — smile at the ready when a teammate might be down. “It’s giving me more confidence to be myself around them and thrive,” Gardner said of the embrace in the locker room. “So it’s just helped me when I got people believing in you, like an organization like this. That’s great. Always.”

title: Kevin Durant admits he's ready if his beef with Dillon Brooks escalates beyond trash talk
summary: Kevin Durant and Dillon Brooks continue to have beef with each other, and it could get even bigger in future games.
content: Kevin Durant admits he's ready if his beef with Dillon Brooks escalates beyond trash talk originally appeared on The Sporting News . Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here . The Houston Rockets got a big win on Wednesday against the Phoenix Suns . During the final possession, the Rockets had already secured the victory. Suns forward Dillon Brooks came up to Kevin Durant to talk some trash. Brooks was promptly ejected from the game due to his second technical foul, while Durant also received one. It was a viral moment for the NBA, as it was true beef between two players that had been brewing for a while. Kevin Durant gets honest about his beef with Dillon Brooks Since he was drafted in 2017, Brooks has relished in the role of being the agitator. He loves getting into his opponents' heads, and since he is a good defender, he loves taking on the opposing team's best player. With that, being matched up against Durant is normal for Brooks. However, they do have a personal beef because they were traded for each other in the 2025 offseason. Since then, Brooks has shown support for Suns owner Mat Ishbia, while throwing shade at Durant. MORE: Dillon Brooks throws some shade after the Suns' win over the Rockets earlier in the 2026-27 season During the game, it seems that it was Brooks who started the confrontation. He had something to say to Durant, and the two-time Finals MVP did not back down from going head-to-head. "I don't mind if somebody got a grievance with me. I don't mind addressing it right there in the moment. I'm sure he has some. I said some things that he probably didn't like, and he addressed it right there, and I respect that as a man. But if it does get farther than that, I'll be ready for that too," Durant said in his post-game press conference . Durant is not the type of person to back down from a clash like this. He came out on top in both the game's result and the bragging rights because he was not ejected from the game. Knowing these two men, it won't be the final chapter in their beef. title: Knicks Clear Three Stars As Heat Face Giannis Probable Status
summary: Jalen Brunson, Karl-Anthony Towns and Josh Hart are cleared for Friday's game. Miami lists Giannis Antetokounmpo as probable with a groin issue.
content: Credit: Sam Navarro-Imagn Images Three New York Knicks stars are cleared to play against the Miami Heat on Friday night. Jalen Brunson, Karl-Anthony Towns and Josh Hart will all see the floor at Madison Square Garden. This news comes after a strong win over the Cleveland Cavaliers on Wednesday. The team now looks healthy for a key Eastern Conference matchup. The Knicks have won six straight games, including three in a row at home. Brunson played 36 minutes in the recent win, while Towns logged 33 minutes. Hart also saw heavy action with 36 minutes of play. Their health is vital for the team’s push up the standings. According to Heavy.com , the core group played a key part in the 121-102 victory. One Major Absence Remains Not everyone is ready to go for New York. OG Anunoby is listed as doubtful due to a left calf strain. He has missed the last three games with this issue. The team might go four games without him if he cannot return soon. New York managed to win those three previous contests despite his absence. In his place, Mikal Bridges and Landry Shamet have taken on more minutes. Against the Cavaliers, no other Knicks player logged more minutes than Bridges. Shamet has continued his improved play this season. Other players like Andre Drummond and Miles McBride are listed as questionable. Their status will be checked closer to tip-off. The roster depth is being tested, but the main stars are back. Giannis Listed as Probable The Miami Heat face their own injury concerns heading into Friday. Giannis Antetokounmpo is listed as probable with right groin tendinitis. The same injury that sidelined him for Sunday’s matchup with the Oklahoma City Thunder is what occurred here. If he plays, he will be the biggest threat to the Knicks. Per Heavy.com, he is averaging 28.4 points and 12.7 rebounds this season. Andrew Wiggins is also listed as probable for the Heat due to a right ankle sprain. The Heat are coming off a loss to the Philadelphia 76ers on Wednesday. They had won seven games in a row before that defeat. LeBron James recorded a triple-double in that loss against Miami. The Heat shot poorly from deep, converting only 5 of 26 three-point attempts. Standings and Stakes New York sits third in the Eastern Conference after their recent win streak. A victory over Miami could help them climb to second place. The Heat have a record of 10-7, while the Knicks are 12-6. Both teams have lost games to Eastern Conference rivals this season. The Knicks have lost all six of their games to both non-conference opponents in this metric however. Charles Barkley offered thoughts on the league during halftime coverage of the Sixers-Heat game. He said missed time for stars could hurt title chances. The Knicks hope their healthy core avoids that fate. The game is set for 7:30 PM ET on Friday.

title: What the Lakers need to do to reach the NBA Cup knockout round
summary: There are several scenarios in which the Lakers would advance to the knockout round of the Emirates NBA Cup.
content: The Los Angeles Lakers will have a big test on Friday when they visit the San Antonio Spurs to start a difficult three-game road trip. While they have the NBA's best record at 15-3, San Antonio is right behind them at 15-4. Friday's game will also be the final NBA Cup group play contest for both teams. It could very well decide which team wins West Group C, although the picture is a bit more complicated than that. For the Lakers to win the group and guarantee themselves a spot in the knockout rounds of the Emirates NBA Cup, they will have to defeat the Spurs and the Portland Trail Blazers will have to beat the Golden State Warriors on Friday. Right now, all four teams are in a tie for first place in West Group C with a 2-1 record in group play. Los Angeles defeated Portland 124-118 on Nov. 6 in group play, giving it the tiebreaker over Portland, but it lost to the Warriors in group play on Oct. 30. The Lakers have to win on Friday to advance to the knockout round. But if they win and the Warriors prevail over Portland, things will become murky. NBA Cup West Group C Friday scenarios: Lakers win group if: - Lakers win at San Antonio AND - Portland wins at home vs. Warriors Getting the West wildcard would be tough for LA at 3-1 given their -9 point differential relative to DAL/DEN (Group A) and MIN/MEM (B) (below): pic.twitter.com/YSS5qRVGO2 — Mike Trudell (@LakersReporter) November 26, 2026 The Lakers are at the bottom of that four-way tie in West Group C with a -9 point differential. That puts them at a disadvantage, as point differential is a major determinant of which team gets the wild-card spot in the knockout round. The three group winners and one wild card in each conference advanced to the first knockout round, which will start on Dec. 4. If the Timberwolves (3-0 in group play) defeat the Memphis Grizzlies (2-1) on Friday, that would leave the Denver Nuggets (2-1) as the one team L.A. would have to beat out. If the Nuggets then lose to the Utah Jazz , Los Angeles would be in. If the Nuggets win, Los Angeles would have to have a higher point differential than the Nuggets, who are currently at -3. A Grizzlies victory would mean that L.A. would have to finish ahead of the Timberwolves. That seems unlikely, as the Timberwolves have a +39 point differential. title: Lights-out Luka and contagious chemistry: are these Lakers for real?
summary: It’s early days, but after a dramatic roster overhaul and an offseason of team-bonding Dončić is playing at an MVP level and LA are looking like contenders
content: Luka Dončić has the Lakers at the top of the Western Conference. Photograph: Gina Ferazzi/Los Angeles Times/Getty Images One of the components of Luka Dončić’s shock trade from the Dallas Mavericks to the Los Angeles Lakers that caused great consternation was that he was just entering his prime as an NBA superstar. The worry was that the move could end that prime before it really even began – unceremoniously uprooting the Slovenian wunderkind from a team custom built around his strengths, fresh off a run to the NBA finals, to one who didn’t really make sense at all. Sure, the bright lights of Hollywood would elevate Dončić’s profile and usher him into a new echelon of stardom. But with Oklahoma City starting their run of dominance and rising stars around the league waiting in the wings, some believed his hopes of title contention (or even a long-elusive MVP award) had vanished. Related: Victor Wembanyama has turned his NBA finals humiliation into a revenge tour for the ages But the start to this season raises the question: what if they were wrong? Dončić is neck-and-neck with Victor Wembanyama in the MVP race, and the Lakers have the best record in the NBA at 15-3, with the Spurs and 76ers just behind at 15-4. San Antonio and their gargantuan French superstar were title and MVP favorites by a wide margin entering this season. But Dončić and the Lakers are keeping pace by pretty much every margin. Friday night’s NBA Cup showdown will be a duel with ripple effects and stakes rarely seen in the regular season, let alone in November. The two top records. The two leading MVP candidates. A basketball fan couldn’t ask for much more. While there’s a general consensus, at least for now, that the MVP race will come down to Dončić and Wembanyama, pundits have been more reluctant to acknowledge the new-look Lakers’ emerging contenderdom. They have hovered near or occupied first place in the Western Conference throughout the season’s first month, and they are top-11 in both offensive and defensive rating. Those are usually the hallmarks of a bona fide contender, but the skepticism persists. Maybe that’s because there was a some dubiousness about the Lakers’ brass pushing their chips in this summer on Walker Kessler, the 25-year-old with alluring talent but a limited résumé, whom the team have slotted as their center of the future. Or perhaps it’s that, aside from Dončić and walking basketball Cinderella story Austin Reaves (who has been sidelined with a heel injury but is slated to return against San Antonio), the roster is lacking in household names. Many of their players, from shooting guard Quentin Grimes to forward Sandro Mamukelashvili, are NBA journeymen, having spent years bouncing around the league looking for the right home. The Lakers turned over 11 of their 15 roster spots this summer, an unusually drastic move for a team coming off a trip to the conference semi-finals and a second straight season with at least 50 wins. But they were committed to building a team around Dončić, and that required a bold approach to overhaul. JJ Redick, the team’s head coach and someone who reportedly played a substantial role in handpicking the roster, acknowledged that turning over essentially the entire team in one offseason is not without its challenges, especially in a market like Los Angeles, where excellence is the goal and immediacy is the decree. “I made this comment to the team after we lost to the Warriors [on 30 October, one of their three defeats to date]: ‘We’ve played six games together. Draymond [Green] and Steph [Curry] have played 13 years together,’” he recalled to me. “Patience is really important. I think one of the things I said in Rob [Pelinka’s] and in my press conference right before Media Day was the belief that this team can become a great team. And that requires patience, that requires a lot of coaching and teaching and buy-in. So that whole process takes time. And you also have to do all of that while playing every other day, or five games in seven nights, and getting results stamped on your forehead every 24 hours. As a human, that’s just hard to do.” The Lakers, by any objective measure, are becoming a great team. They may not be one yet (the bout with the Spurs will be their first real test after a soft early schedule) but they appear well on their way. There are several factors to point to – chief among them Dončić’s historic scoring pace – but buy-in and chemistry should not be overlooked. It started, Redick and several team members tell me, on a team bonding trip to Slovenia this summer where Dončić began to level up as a leader. He self-funded the trip, expediting the bonding process with such a new group while also letting his teammates see his origin story. It was widely appreciated, and proved effective. With a group of eager role-players immediately willing to buy into Dončić and Redick’s vision, friction has been at a minimum, and roles slotted into with relative ease. “When we started training camp, I saw a lot of potential in this team,” Dončić said after an overtime win against the Charlotte Hornets. “At the end of the day we have great chemistry, which is, in my opinion, very important. But I think this group is very special.” His teammate Collin Sexton, one of the aforementioned journeymen, agrees. “We’re gelling a lot faster than anyone could’ve expected. That’s something that’s helping us win games,” he said. “That camaraderie, and that togetherness is something that’s going to continue to allow us to expedite the friendships on the court, but also off the court.” Related: Giannis says Dončić could be best scorer of all time as Lakers star pours in 42 against Heat I asked Redick why he thinks the group has been able to gel so quickly. He immediately recalled a team dinner he hosted in Las Vegas at Carbone Riviera, the night before a preseason contest in October. It was a two-plus-hour dinner, and when the checks came he looked around and noticed something. “I get up to leave, and it struck me: nobody had left. Nobody had been on their phone,” he said. “Part of this, beyond just the time spent together [in Slovenia and in the lead-up to the season], is the people in there – the people in that locker room. It’s just, they want to be part of a special group.” Fresh off two “successful” regular seasons that ended in playoff disappointment, Redick makes a point to acknowledge that it’s still early: “I don’t know what this is going to look like after 82 games. I don’t know what it’s going to look like after 50. But I do know that there’s something with this group. And every special group doesn’t mean you win a championship. But it’s a special group of guys.” No contender can summit the mountaintop on the power of friendship alone, so it really does, ultimately, come back to Dončić’s brilliance. His teammates understand this, and are leaning into their jobs as supporting actors in his quest for his first proverbial Best Actor and Best Picture. Kessler, chuckling and shaking his head after another night of his teammate’s dominance, stated definitively after Dončić’s 53-point outburst against the Portland Trail Blazers this month: “He’s my MVP, I think it’s pretty clear right now.” Time will tell if these Lakers really have what it takes to win it all. But in a wide-open Western Conference, with everything seemingly falling into place faster than most imagined, they’re operating with the ethos of a popular refrain: “Why not us?”

Try to stay off of it as much as possible. … There’s not really a certain thing you can do to make the process speed up, you kind of just got to let time take care of those things.” Reaves added that seeing the Spurs on their schedule motivated him to return as quickly as possible. However, he was adamant about not risking his health by coming back at less than 100 percent.
